facts.fact: Villa La Rotonda is a Renaissance villa outside Vicenza designed by Andrea Palladio, begun in 1567 and not completed until 1605.
facts.quote: Villa La Rotonda is a Renaissance villa just outside Vicenza in Northern Italy designed by Italian Renaissance architect Andrea Palladio, and begun in 1567, though not completed until 1605.

facts.fact: The villa is completely symmetrical: a square plan with four facades, each with a projecting portico.
facts.quote: The design is for a completely symmetrical building having a square plan with four facades, each of which has a projecting portico.

facts.fact: The name La Rotonda refers to the central circular hall with its dome.
facts.quote: The name La Rotonda refers to the central circular hall with its dome.

facts.fact: Each portico's pediment carries statues of classical deities and rests on six Ionic columns.
facts.quote: Each of the four porticos has pediments graced by statues of classical deities. The pediments were each supported by six Ionic columns.

facts.fact: The design was rotated 45 degrees from the cardinal points so that every room gets some sun.
facts.quote: In order for each room to have some sun, the design was rotated 45 degrees from each cardinal point of the compass.

facts.fact: After Palladio died in 1580, Vincenzo Scamozzi was employed to oversee the completion.
facts.quote: Palladio died in 1580 and a second architect, Vincenzo Scamozzi, was employed by the new owners to oversee the completion.

facts.fact: Palladio intended a high semi-circular dome, but Scamozzi built a lower dome with an oculus inspired by the Pantheon in Rome.
facts.quote: Palladio had intended it to be covered by a high semi-circular dome but Scamozzi designed a lower dome with an oculus (intended to be open to the sky) inspired by the Pantheon in Rome.

facts.fact: The villa is part of the World Heritage Site "City of Vicenza and the Palladian Villas of the Veneto".
facts.quote: Along with other works by Palladio, the building is conserved as part of the World Heritage Site "City of Vicenza and the Palladian Villas of the Veneto".

facts.fact: The Walt Disney Concert Hall in downtown Los Angeles was designed by Frank Gehry and opened on 23 October 2003.
facts.quote: The Walt Disney Concert Hall in downtown Los Angeles, California, is the fourth hall of the Los Angeles Music Center and was designed by Frank Gehry. It was opened on October 23, 2003.

facts.fact: It seats 2,265 people and is home to the Los Angeles Philharmonic and the Los Angeles Master Chorale.
facts.quote: Bounded by Hope Street, Grand Avenue, and 1st and 2nd streets, it seats 2,265 people and serves, among other purposes, as the home of the Los Angeles Philharmonic orchestra and the Los Angeles Master Chorale.

facts.fact: The hall is a compromise between vineyard-style seating, like Scharoun's Berliner Philharmonie, and a classical shoebox.
facts.quote: The hall is a compromise between a vineyard-style seating configuration, like the Berliner Philharmonie by Hans Scharoun, and a classical shoebox design like the Vienna Musikverein or the Boston Symphony Hall.

facts.fact: The hall's acoustics were designed by Minoru Nagata, with Yasuhisa Toyota supervising completion, and have been praised.
facts.quote: Both Gehry's architecture and the acoustics of the concert hall, designed by Minoru Nagata, the final completion supervised by Nagata's assistant and protege Yasuhisa Toyota, have been praised, in contrast to its predecessor, the Dorothy Chandler Pavilion.

facts.fact: To save money, the stone exterior first designed was replaced with a cheaper stainless steel skin.
facts.quote: Plans were revised, and in a cost-saving move the originally designed stone exterior was replaced with a less costly stainless steel skin.

facts.fact: Gehry used CATIA, software normally used to design French fighter jets, to make the complex design buildable.
facts.quote: The technology, called CATIA (computer-aided three-dimensional interactive application) is typically used in the design process for French fighter jets, but its mathematical ability aided Gehry in his process of designing the Walt Disney Concert Hall.

facts.fact: Gehry used the angular design to "symbolize musical movement and the motion of Los Angeles".
facts.quote: The angular design was used by Gehry to "symbolize musical movement and the motion of Los Angeles".

facts.fact: Inside, the walls and ceiling of the hall are Douglas fir and the floor is oak.
facts.quote: The walls and ceiling of the hall are finished with Douglas-fir while the floor is finished with oak.

facts.fact: The museum's Main Building was designed by Le Corbusier, his only representative work in the Far East.
facts.quote: The Main Building was designed by the Swiss-French architect Le Corbusier.  It is the only representative example of his work in the Far East; and the New York Times review of its opening suggested that the building itself presented an "artistic significance and beauty" which rivaled the paintings inside.

facts.fact: The reinforced concrete building was completed in March 1959 as a symbol of renewed diplomatic ties between Japan and France after World War II.
facts.quote: The multi-story, reinforced concrete building was completed in March 1959 as a symbol of the resumption of diplomatic ties between Japan and France after World War II.

facts.fact: Le Corbusier's three Japanese apprentices, Kunio Maekawa, Junzo Sakakura and Takamasa Yoshizaka, developed the detailed drawings and supervised construction.
facts.quote: Le Corbusier asked that his three Japanese apprentices: Kunio Maekawa, Junzo Sakakura and Takamasa Yoshizaka be responsible for developing the detailed drawings and supervising the construction.

facts.fact: The museum is square in plan with its galleries raised on pilotis; the layout is influenced by his Sanskar Kendra museum in Ahmedabad.
facts.quote: The museum is square in plan, with the main body of the galleries raised on piloti to first floor level. The layout is influenced by Le Corbusier's Sanskar Kendra museum in Ahmedabad which was being designed at the same time.

facts.fact: Visitors enter the double-height 19th Century Hall, lit from above by a north-glazed pyramidal skylight.
facts.quote: Entrance for visitors is at ground floor level via the 19th Century Hall. This double height space is lit from above with a north glazed pyramidal skylight intersected with reinforced concrete beams and a column.

facts.fact: The paintings gallery was designed to be lit by daylight through four lighting troughs, which are no longer used.
facts.quote: Le Corbusier designed the paintings gallery to be lit by natural daylight via four lighting troughs, but these are no longer used, and the galleries are now artificially lit.

facts.fact: Outside, the building is clad in prefabricated concrete panels.
facts.quote: Externally, the building is clad in prefabricated concrete panels which sit on U-shaped frames supported by the inner wall.

facts.fact: In July 2016 UNESCO listed the building among 17 works by Le Corbusier as World Heritage Sites.
facts.quote: In July 2016 UNESCO listed 17 works by Le Corbusier as World Heritage Sites, including the 1959 National Museum of Western Art building.

facts.fact: The NMAAHC is a Smithsonian Institution museum on the National Mall in Washington, D.C.
facts.quote: The National Museum of African American History and Culture (NMAAHC), colloquially known as the Blacksonian, is a Smithsonian Institution museum located on the National Mall in Washington, D.C., in the United States.

facts.fact: A design by Freelon Group/Adjaye Associates/Davis Brody Bond was chosen in 2009; construction ran from 2012 to 2016.
facts.quote: A site was selected in 2006, and a design submitted by Freelon Group/Adjaye Associates/Davis Brody Bond was chosen in 2009. Construction began in 2012 and was completed in 2016.

facts.fact: The 350,000-square-foot building has ten storeys, five above ground and five below.
facts.quote: The 350,000-square-foot (33,000 m2), 10-story building (five above and five below ground) and its exhibits have won critical praise.

facts.fact: The building had to be LEED Gold certified and meet strict federal security standards.
facts.quote: The building was limited to the 5-acre (20,000 m2) site chosen by the site selection committee, had to be LEED Gold certified, and had to meet stringent federal security standards.

facts.fact: The upper floors form an inverted step pyramid wrapped in a bronze scrim, reflecting a Yoruba crown and inspired by an Olowe of Ise sculpture.
facts.quote: The above-ground floors featured an inverted step pyramid surrounded by a bronze architectural scrim, which reflected an Oba's crown as used in Yoruba culture; specifically, these three stacked trapezoidal shapes were inspired by the top of an Olowe of Ise sculpture which is now on display inside the museum.

facts.fact: The scrim's perforated patterns are based on historic iron grilles in African-American communities in Charleston and New Orleans.
facts.quote: The exterior of this structure, whose frames lean outward to create the corona, consisted of a thin screen or "scrim" perforated by geometrical patterns based on historic iron grilles found in African-American communities in Charleston, South Carolina, and New Orleans, Louisiana.

facts.fact: A 200 ft long-span porch built of plate girders and box columns covers the main entrance.
facts.quote: The 200 ft (61 m) long-span porch that covers the main entrance was built of long plate girders and box columns (also made of plate).

facts.fact: The museum won the architecture category and was overall winner of the Beazley Design of the Year award for 2017.
facts.quote: ArchDaily has reported that the museum was named the winner for the architecture category and the overall winner for the Beazley Design of the Year award for 2017.

facts.fact: Guangzhou Opera House is a public municipal opera house designed by Zaha Hadid; it opened on 9 May 2010.
facts.quote: Guangzhou Opera House (广州大剧院) is a public municipal opera house in Guangzhou, Guangdong, China. Designed by Zaha Hadid, it opened on 9 May in 2010.

facts.fact: Hadid's "double pebble" won the 2002 competition, and ground was broken early in 2005.
facts.quote: In November 2002, Zaha Hadid's "double pebble" was announced the winner and the groundbreaking ceremony was held early in 2005.

facts.fact: The building is conceived as two rocks washed away by the Pearl River.
facts.quote: The structure was designed by Iraqi architect Zaha Hadid. It is conceived as two rocks washed away by the Pearl River.

facts.fact: A freestanding concrete auditorium sits within an exposed granite and glass-clad steel frame that took over five years to build.
facts.quote: Its freestanding concrete auditorium set within an exposed granite and glass-clad steel frame took over five years to build, and was praised upon opening by architectural critic Jonathan Glancey in The Guardian, who called it "at once highly theatrical and insistently subtle."

facts.fact: It looks like two smooth-edged boulders faced with 75,000 panels of polished granite and glass.
facts.quote: It appears akin to two giant smooth-edged boulders faced with 75,000 panels of polished granite and glass.

facts.fact: The complex holds an 1,800-seat theatre, a multipurpose theatre, an entry hall and a salon, with a covered pathway between the two main structures.
facts.quote: The complex comprises an 1,800-seat theatre, a multipurpose theatre, entry hall, and salon. A covered pathway with restaurants and shops separates the two main structures.

facts.fact: It stands in a new business district of the city, with a 103-storey glass tower behind it.
facts.quote: The Guangzhou Opera House is located in a new business district of the city, with a new 103-storey glass tower behind it.

facts.fact: It has become the biggest performing centre in southern China.
facts.quote: The theatre has become the biggest performing centre in southern China and is one of the three biggest theatres in the nation alongside Beijing's National Centre for the Performing Arts and Shanghai's Shanghai Grand Theatre.

facts.fact: The building is the home of the Scottish Parliament at Holyrood in Edinburgh; construction began in June 1999 and the first debate there was held on 7 September 2004.
facts.quote: The Scottish Parliament Building is the home of the Scottish Parliament at Holyrood in central Edinburgh. Construction of the building commenced in June 1999 and the Members of the Scottish Parliament (MSPs) held their first debate in the new building on 7 September 2004.

facts.fact: Its architect, Enric Miralles, died before it was completed.
facts.quote: Enric Miralles, the controversial Spanish architect who designed the building, died before its completion.

facts.fact: It won the 2005 Stirling Prize among numerous awards.
facts.quote: The Parliament Building won numerous awards including the 2005 Stirling Prize and has been described by landscape architect Charles Jencks as "a tour de force of arts and crafts and quality without parallel in the last 100 years of British architecture".

facts.fact: Links to nature include leaf-shaped roof motifs over the Garden Lobby and large windows facing Holyrood Park, Arthur's Seat and Salisbury Crags.
facts.quote: As a consequence, the building has many features connected to nature and land, such as the leaf shaped motifs of the roof in the Garden Lobby of the building, and the large windows of the debating chamber, committee rooms and the Tower Buildings, which face the broad expanse of Holyrood Park, Arthur's Seat and Salisbury Crags.

facts.fact: Inside, Scottish gneiss and granite are used in floors and walls, and oak and sycamore in the furniture.
facts.quote: Inside the buildings, the connection to the land is reinforced by the use of Scottish rock, such as gneiss and granite in the flooring and walls, and the use of oak and sycamore in the construction of the furniture.

facts.fact: The debating chamber roof rests on laminated oak beams joined by 112 stainless steel connectors and hung on steel rods from the walls.
facts.quote: The roof is supported by a structure of laminated oak beams joined with a total of 112 stainless steel connectors (each slightly different), which in turn are suspended on steel rods from the walls.

facts.fact: The MSP offices have projecting bay windows with a seat and shelving, meant as "contemplation spaces".
facts.quote: The most distinctive feature of the MSP block are the unusual windows which project out from the building onto the western elevation of the parliamentary complex, inspired by a combination of the repeated leaf motif and the traditional Scottish stepped gable. In each office, these bay windows have a seat and shelving and are intended as "contemplation spaces".

facts.fact: In summer the windows open at night so the heavy concrete floors and structure can cool.
facts.quote: During summer months, the building opens the windows during the night time when it is unoccupied and permits the heavy concrete floors and structure to cool and rid themselves of heat absorbed during the day.

facts.fact: Lever House is a 307-foot office building on Park Avenue in Manhattan, built 1950–1952 to designs by Gordon Bunshaft and Natalie de Blois of SOM in the International Style.
facts.quote: Lever House is a 307-foot-tall (94 m) office building at 390 Park Avenue in the Midtown Manhattan neighborhood of Manhattan in New York City, United States. Constructed from 1950 to 1952, the building was designed by Gordon Bunshaft and Natalie de Blois of Skidmore, Owings & Merrill (SOM) in the International Style, a 20th-century modern architectural style.

facts.fact: It was the headquarters of Lever Brothers and the second New York high-rise with a glass curtain wall, after the UN Secretariat.
facts.quote: It was originally the headquarters of soap company Lever Brothers, a subsidiary of Unilever. Lever House was the second high-rise in New York City with a glass curtain wall, after the United Nations Secretariat Building.

facts.fact: The ground floor is a courtyard and public space; the second floor overhangs the plaza on columns, and the slab above covers the northern quarter of the site.
facts.quote: At the ground story is a courtyard and public space, with the second story overhanging the plaza on a set of columns. The remaining stories are designed as a slab occupying the northern one-quarter of the site.

facts.fact: The slab met the 1916 Zoning Resolution without setbacks.
facts.quote: The slab design was chosen because it conformed with the city's 1916 Zoning Resolution while avoiding the use of setbacks.

facts.fact: Its glass-and-metal facade follows Mies, while the courtyard raised on stilts follows Le Corbusier.
facts.quote: The building's glass-and-metal facade was similar to Mies's designs, while its raised-on-stilts courtyard was influenced by Le Corbusier's teachings.

facts.fact: Above the ground floor every facade is a curtain wall of heat-absorbing glass and stainless steel.
facts.quote: Above the ground floor, all elevations of the facade contain a curtain wall with heat-absorbing glass panes and stainless steel.

facts.fact: Lever House turned Park Avenue into an avenue of International-style offices, and other buildings worldwide copied it.
facts.quote: The construction of Lever House changed Park Avenue in Midtown from an avenue with masonry apartment buildings to one with International-style office buildings. Several other structures worldwide copied the building's design.

facts.fact: Nearly demolished in the 1980s, it became a New York City landmark in 1982 and was added to the National Register of Historic Places the next year.
facts.quote: The building was nearly demolished in the 1980s, when Fisher Brothers proposed a 40-story tower on the site; afterward, it was narrowly approved as a New York City designated landmark in 1982 and was added to the National Register of Historic Places the next year.

facts.fact: Torre Velasca is a Milan skyscraper by the BBPR partnership, completed in 1958 and inaugurated in 1961.
facts.quote: The Torre Velasca ("Velasca Tower") is a skyscraper built in the 1950s by the BBPR architectural partnership, in Milan, Italy. The construction was achieved in 1958, and  inaugurated in 1961.

facts.fact: It is 106 metres tall with 26 storeys and is considered a rare Italian example of post-rationalist brutalism.
facts.quote: Measuring 106 metres (348 ft) in height to the roof, the tower has 26 stories. The building is considered one of the few Italian examples of post-rationalist brutalist architecture.

facts.fact: Its mushroom-like shape recalls the massive medieval fortresses and towers of Lombardy.
facts.quote: The Torre Velasca is known for its peculiar and characteristic mushroom-like shape that stands out in the city skyline. Its structure recalls the Lombard tradition, made of medieval fortresses and towers, each having a massive profile.

facts.fact: The shape also met functional needs: narrower floors at the bottom, wider ones at the top.
facts.quote: At the same time, BBPR in this building satisfied the functional needs of space: narrower surfaces on the ground, wider and more spacious ones on the top floors.

facts.fact: A first steel-and-glass scheme was dropped for cost, and BBPR used a reinforced concrete structure with stone cladding instead.
facts.quote: Due to the high cost of the material and the national production capacity of the time, this initial proposal was abandoned; BBPR instead opted for a reinforced concrete structure with stone cladding.

facts.fact: Its cantilevered upper section on exposed diagonal trusses draws on Lombard fortresses and the Filarete Tower of the Castello Sforzesco.
facts.quote: Its cantilevered upper section supported by exposed diagonal trusses drew deliberate inspiration from late-medieval Lombard fortresses and the Filarete Tower of the Castello Sforzesco.

facts.fact: In 1961 BBPR received the IN/ARCH Regional Award for Lombardy for the design.
facts.quote: Conversely, the Italian architectural community recognized its contextual dialogue; in 1961, BBPR received the Regional Award for Lombardy from the National Institute of Architecture (IN/ARCH) for the design.

facts.fact: In 2011 the tower was placed under protection as a historic building.
facts.quote: In 2011, the tower was placed under protection as a historic building.

facts.fact: The Louvre Pyramid is a large glass-and-metal entrance and skylight designed by I. M. Pei.
facts.quote: The Louvre Pyramid (French: Pyramide du Louvre) is a large glass-and-metal entrance way and skylight designed by the Chinese-American architect I. M. Pei.

facts.fact: It is the museum's main entrance, lighting the underground visitors' hall that leads to the palace's different wings.
facts.quote: The large pyramid serves as the main entrance way to the Louvre Museum, allowing light to the below ground visitors hall, while also allowing sight lines of the palace to visitors in the hall, and through access galleries to the different wings of the palace.

facts.fact: It was completed in 1989 as part of the Grand Louvre project and has become a landmark of Paris.
facts.quote: Completed in 1989 as part of the broader Grand Louvre project, it has become a landmark of Paris and a symbol of the museum.

facts.fact: François Mitterrand announced the Grand Louvre project in 1981, and Pei was selected as architect in 1983.
facts.quote: The Grand Louvre project was announced in 1981 by François Mitterrand, the president of France. In 1983 the Chinese-American architect I. M. Pei was selected as its architect.

facts.fact: Built entirely of glass segments and metal poles, it is 21.6 metres high on a square base with 34-metre sides.
facts.quote: Constructed entirely with glass segments and metal poles, it reaches a height of 21.6 metres (71 ft). Its square base has sides of 34 metres (112 ft) and a base surface area of 1,000 square metres (11,000 ft2).

facts.fact: Its sides rise at 51.52 degrees, similar to ancient Egyptian pyramids.
facts.quote: The sides' angle relative to the base is 51.52 degrees, an angle similar to that of ancient Egyptian pyramids.

facts.fact: The pyramid and underground lobby were built because the old layout could no longer handle the growing number of visitors.
facts.quote: The pyramid and the underground lobby were constructed to address limitations in the Louvre's previous layout, which was no longer capable of accommodating the steadily growing number of daily visitors.

facts.fact: Its construction set off years of aesthetic and political debate.
facts.quote: The construction of the pyramid triggered many years of lively aesthetic and political debate.

facts.fact: The museum stands in Flamengo Park in Rio de Janeiro, on Guanabara Bay.
facts.quote: The Museum of Modern Art of Rio de Janeiro (Portuguese: Museu de Arte Moderna do Rio de Janeiro, MAM) is a museum located in northeastern Flamengo Park, in the city of Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. It is in the Centro district, west of Santos Dumont Airport, on Guanabara Bay.

facts.fact: The Modernist concrete building was designed by Affonso Eduardo Reidy, with Carmen Portinho as chief engineer; its gardens are by Burle Marx.
facts.quote: The Modernist concrete museum building, designed by Affonso Eduardo Reidy (1909-1964) with his partner Carmen Portinho serving as chief engineer, was completed in 1955. The museum's landmark Modernist gardens were designed by Burle Marx.

facts.fact: A row of external pillars joined by long beams gives a gallery level free of internal columns or structural walls.
facts.quote: The main building has a dramatic cadence of external pillar elements, connected by longitudinal beams, providing a galley level free of internal columns or structural walls.

facts.fact: Because the park sits on landfill in the bay, the pillar footings reach 20 metres down.
facts.quote: The park was created on landfill in the bay, so the pillars footings reach 20 metres (66 ft) down.

facts.fact: Aluminium shutters on the north facade control the low winter light entering the galleries, whose windows face north and south.
facts.quote: The northern façade has aluminum shutters to control the amount of (low) natural light entering the gallery space during the winter solstice period. The windows of the gallery are oriented to the north and south.

facts.fact: A broad spiral ramp leads up to a roof terrace overlooking Guanabara Bay and Sugarloaf.
facts.quote: A broad spiral ramp element reaches an upper level, with a roof terrace, restaurant, bar, and lounge overlooking Guanabara Bay, Sugarloaf, and Rio's other granitic mountain formations.

facts.fact: A fire on 8 July 1978 destroyed 90% of the museum's collection.
facts.quote: On July 8, 1978, a fire caused either by a cigarette or an electrical failure destroyed 90% of the museum's collection, including artworks from Pablo Picasso ("Cubist Head" and "Portrait of Dora Maar"), Joan Miró ("Persons in a Landscape"), Salvador Dalí ("Egg on a Plate, Without the Plate"), Max Ernst, Paul Klee, Diego Rivera, René Magritte, Louis Van Lint, Ivan Serpa, David Alfaro Siqueiros, Manabu Mabe and others – and all artworks showed in a big retrospective of artist Joaquín Torres-García.

facts.fact: It is the military museum of the German Armed Forces, the Bundeswehr.
facts.quote: The Bundeswehr Military History Museum (German: Militärhistorisches Museum der Bundeswehr (MHMBw)) is the military museum of the German Armed Forces, the Bundeswehr, and one of the major military history museums in Germany.

facts.fact: The museum is in a former military arsenal in Dresden's Albertstadt.
facts.quote: It is located in a former military arsenal in the Albertstadt which is part of Dresden.

facts.fact: The original armoury was built between 1873 and 1876 and became a museum in 1897.
facts.quote: The original building, the armory, was built between 1873 and 1876 and became a museum in 1897.

facts.fact: A 2001 competition sought an extension that would make visitors rethink how they think about war.
facts.quote: By 2001, feelings regarding the museum had shifted and an architectural competition was held for an extension which would cause visitors to reconsider the way they think about war.

facts.fact: After six years of construction it reopened in October 2011, with Daniel Libeskind's transparent arrowhead added to the facade.
facts.quote: Before opening in October 2011 as the Bundeswehr Military History Museum, the building underwent six years of extensive construction. Jewish architect Daniel Libeskind added a transparent arrowhead to the façade of the building, creating, according to the Dresden Tourism board, "an outwardly visible expression of innovation".

facts.fact: Libeskind's studio says the open, transparent new facade stands for democratic society, against the rigid old building of the authoritarian past.
facts.quote: Libeskind's studio states that "the openness and transparency of the new façade, representing the openness of democratic society, contrasts with the rigidity of the existing building, which represents the severity of the authoritarian past".

facts.fact: The silver arrowhead holds a five-storey, 29-metre viewing platform that points toward where the fire bombing of Dresden began.
facts.quote: The silver arrowhead protrudes from the center of the traditional Neo-Classical building and provides a five-story, 29 meter high viewing platform which overlooks the city. The platform provides views of modern Dresden while pointing towards the area where the fire bombings of Dresden began.

facts.fact: The museum focuses on the human side of war as well as German military technology.
facts.quote: The museum focuses on the human aspects of war, while also showcasing the evolution of German military technology.

facts.fact: Auguste Perret and his studio led the rebuilding of Le Havre after the city was destroyed in World War II.
facts.quote: From 1945 to 1964, the City of Le Havre commissioned Auguste Perret and his studio to head the rebuilding of the entire city after it had been completely destroyed by the British during World War II.

facts.fact: St. Joseph's was built between 1951 and 1957/58 as part of the reconstruction and is a memorial to the five thousand civilians who died.
facts.quote: St. Joseph's was built between 1951 and 1957/58 as part of this reconstruction. It acts as a memorial to the five thousand civilians fallen and the usual sanctuary dedicated to a patron saint; in this case Saint Joseph, fittingly the patron saint of a happy death, fathers, workers, travelers, and immigrants.

facts.fact: The centrally planned church was envisioned as a beacon, its single central tower dominating the skyline.
facts.quote: A centrally-planned building, Saint Joseph's Church was envisioned as a beacon for the city. The church's single, central tower dominates the city skyline, easily visible from the city's port.

facts.fact: Built of concrete, its tower is 107 metres tall and visible from the sea, especially when lit at night.
facts.quote: Made of concrete, St Joseph's is a product of modern architectural innovation in Post-War France. The tower is 107 meters tall and acts as a beacon visible from out at sea, especially at night when illuminated.

facts.fact: Perret brought in Marguerite Huré for the stained glass.
facts.quote: Perret brought in his previous colleague Marguerite Huré (1896–1967) for the stained glass in the new church.

facts.fact: From seven base colours Huré made fifty different hues.
facts.quote: Using a selection of seven primary colors (orange, yellow, green, purple, red, greenish and white), Huré manipulated each base color to make a total of fifty different hues.

facts.fact: The glass is strongest at the bottom of the tower and lightens toward the top, so the light seems to come from above.
facts.quote: The bottom of the tower has the strongest harmonized hues that gradually lighten on the way to the top giving the impression that the light comes from above, through the lighter glass.

facts.fact: In 2005 UNESCO declared Perret's reconstruction of Le Havre a World Heritage Site.
facts.quote: In 2005, his reconstruction of Le Havre was declared a World Heritage Site by UNESCO.

facts.fact: It holds the largest and most comprehensive collection of British art outside the United Kingdom.
facts.quote: The Yale Center for British Art at Yale University in central New Haven, Connecticut, United States, houses the largest and most comprehensive collection of British art outside the United Kingdom.

facts.fact: The center was founded through Paul Mellon's 1966 gift of his British art collection, with funds for a building.
facts.quote: The center was established by a gift from Paul Mellon (Yale College Class of 1929) of his British art collection to Yale in 1966, together with an endowment for operations of the center, and funds for a building to house the artworks.

facts.fact: Louis Kahn designed it, across the street from his early Yale University Art Gallery of 1953.
facts.quote: The building was designed by Louis I. Kahn and constructed at the corner of York and Chapel Streets in New Haven, across the street from one of Kahn's earliest buildings, the Yale University Art Gallery, built in 1953.

facts.fact: It was completed after Kahn's death in 1974 and opened on 15 April 1977.
facts.quote: The Yale Center for British Art was completed after Kahn's death in 1974, and opened to the public on April 15, 1977.

facts.fact: The exterior is matte steel and reflective glass; inside are travertine marble, white oak and Belgian linen.
facts.quote: The exterior is made of matte steel and reflective glass; the interior is made of travertine marble, white oak, and Belgian linen.

facts.fact: Kahn made intimate galleries in diffused natural light, using artificial light only on dark days or in the evening.
facts.quote: Kahn succeeded in creating intimate galleries where one can view objects in diffused natural light. He wanted to allow in as much daylight as possible, with artificial illumination used only on dark days or in the evening.

facts.fact: The center is open to the public free of charge six days a week.
facts.quote: The center is open to the public free of charge six days a week, and is a member of the North American Reciprocal Museums program.

facts.fact: The National Museum of Qatar in Doha opened its current building on 28 March 2019.
facts.quote: The National Museum of Qatar is a national museum in Doha, Qatar. The current building opened to the public on 28 March 2019, replacing the previous building which opened in 1975.

facts.fact: Jean Nouvel designed it, inspired by the desert rose crystal found in Qatar.
facts.quote: The building was designed by the French architect Jean Nouvel who was inspired by the desert rose crystal, which is found in Qatar.

facts.fact: The new building grows around the early 20th-century palace of Sheikh Abdullah bin Jassim Al Thani.
facts.quote: The new building was constructed on the site of the old building. It was designed by Pritzker Prize-winning architect Jean Nouvel who was inspired by the desert rose and grows around the original twentieth-century palace of Sheikh Abdullah bin Jassim Al Thani.

facts.fact: The historic palace was restored by the Berlin firm ZRS Architekten Ingenieure.
facts.quote: The historic palace was restored by Berlin-based architecture and engineering firm ZRS Architekten Ingenieure.

facts.fact: The 40,000 m² museum is made of interlocking discs that create cavities to shield visitors from the desert heat.
facts.quote: The 430,000 square foot (40,000 m2) museum is made up of interlocking discs that create cavities to protect visitors from the desert heat.

facts.fact: It has 539 intertwined discs clad in about 76,000 glass-fibre-reinforced concrete panels.
facts.quote: The building is made up of 539 intertwined discs, and its glass-fiber-reinforced concrete cladding consists of about 76,000 panels.

facts.fact: At the south end of Doha's Corniche, the building rises from the sea and is linked to the shore by bridges.
facts.quote: Located on a 1.5 million ft² site at the south end of Doha's Corniche, the NMoQ building rises from the sea and is connected to the shore by two pedestrian bridges and a road bridge.

facts.fact: When it reopened it held LEED Gold certification.
facts.quote: At the time of the museum's reopening, the project held a LEED Gold certification and a four-star Global Sustainability Assessment System rating.

facts.fact: Saint-Pierre is a concrete building in Firminy, France, and the last major work of Le Corbusier, completed in 2006, forty-one years after his death.
facts.quote: Saint-Pierre (English: Saint Peter) is a concrete building in the commune of Firminy, France. The last major work of  Le Corbusier, it was started in 1973 and completed in 2006, forty-one years after his death.

facts.fact: It was designed as a church for the model town of Firminy Vert, and building began after Le Corbusier's death in 1965.
facts.quote: Designed to be a church in the model city of Firminy Vert, the construction of Saint-Pierre was begun in 1971, six years after Le Corbusier's death in 1965.

facts.fact: Work stalled from 1975 to 2003, when the local government declared the concrete ruin "architectural heritage" and paid for its completion.
facts.quote: Due to local political conflicts it remained stalled from 1975 to 2003, when the local government declared the mouldering concrete ruin an "architectural heritage" and financed its completion.

facts.fact: It was completed by José Oubrerie, Le Corbusier's long-time student.
facts.quote: The building was completed by the French architect José Oubrerie, Le Corbusier's student for many years.

facts.fact: Because the French state may not fund religious buildings, it is used as a cultural venue.
facts.quote: As the secularist French state may not use public funds for religious buildings, Saint-Pierre is now used as a cultural venue.

facts.fact: Vanity Fair's 2010 World Architecture Survey ranked it second among the top buildings of the 21st century.
facts.quote: In the World Architecture Survey of 2010, by Vanity Fair magazine, the building was ranked as second in the rankings of the top structures built in the twenty-first century, receiving four votes.

facts.fact: Peter Eisenman called it the most important structure built since 1980.
facts.quote: American deconstructionist architect Peter Eisenman asserted in his response that this building is the most important structure built since 1980.

facts.fact: The Oakland Museum of California covers the art, history and natural science of California.
facts.quote: The Oakland Museum of California or OMCA (formerly the Oakland Museum) is an interdisciplinary museum dedicated to the art, history, and natural science of California, located at 1000 Oak Street in Oakland, California.

facts.fact: It was founded in 1969 by merging three smaller Oakland museums.
facts.quote: The OMCA was founded in 1969 as a merger of three smaller area museums – the Oakland Public Museum, the Oakland Art Gallery, and the Snow Museum of Natural History.

facts.fact: A 1961 bond issue started the development of its campus overlooking Lake Merritt.
facts.quote: This plan was eventually realized in 1961 when voters approved a $6.6 million bond issue to start the development of what would become the OMCA campus overlooking Lake Merritt in the city center.

facts.fact: The building is by Kevin Roche John Dinkeloo and Associates, with landscape by Dan Kiley, and is an important example of mid-century modernism joining indoors and outdoors.
facts.quote: The museum building, designed by architect Kevin Roche John Dinkeloo and Associates LLC (Roche-Dinkeloo), with landscape design by Dan Kiley and gardens by Geraldine Knight Scott, is an important example of mid-century modernism and the integration of indoor and outdoor spaces.

facts.fact: The concrete building has three tiers, one each for art, history and natural science.
facts.quote: The concrete building includes three tiers, one each focusing on the art, history, and natural science collections, along with temporary exhibition galleries, an auditorium, a restaurant, and other ancillary spaces.

facts.fact: Outside are terraced roof gardens, patios, sculpture, a lawn and a koi pond.
facts.quote: Outdoor architectural features are terraced roof gardens, patios, outdoor sculpture, a large lawn area, and a koi pond.

facts.fact: It was Roche and Dinkeloo's first major commission, designed with interrelated terraces and roof gardens.
facts.quote: Following this, Roche and Dinkeloo's first major commission was the Oakland Museum of California, a complex for the art, natural history, and cultural history of California with a design featuring interrelated terraces and roof gardens.

facts.fact: Mark Cavagnero Associates designed a major renovation and expansion between 2009 and 2013.
facts.quote: Between 2009 and 2013, the museum underwent a major renovation and expansion designed by Mark Cavagnero Associates.

facts.fact: Kaleva Church is a Lutheran church in Tampere, designed by Reima and Raili Pietilä and built in 1964–66.
facts.quote: Kaleva Church (Finnish: Kalevan kirkko; Swedish: Kalevakyrkan) is an Evangelical Lutheran Church of Finland church building in the Liisankallio district of Tampere, Finland. It was designed by Reima and Raili Pietilä and built in 1964–66.

facts.fact: Reima Pietilä won the 1959 competition; his partner and later wife Raili joined the project.
facts.quote: In 1959, the board of the Evangelical Lutheran Churches in Tampere announced a competition to design a church building for the parish. The entry selected was by architect Reima Pietilä, whose architectural partner (and, from 1963, wife) Raili Paatelainen later became involved in the project.

facts.fact: The church stands on a small hill where two major Tampere streets meet.
facts.quote: The site chosen for the church was a small hill at the head of the convergence of two of Tampere's major streets: Teiskontie and Sammonkatu.

facts.fact: It was slip-formed from 17 narrow, 35-metre-high hollow concrete U-shapes with full-height windows between them.
facts.quote: The building was constructed using slip forming. It is made from 17 narrow 35 m (115 ft)-high hollow concrete u-shapes, with full height windows between them.

facts.fact: The floor plan resembles a fish, an ancient Christian symbol; the main hall is 30 metres high and seats 1,120.
facts.quote: The floor plan of the church resembles a fish, an ancient symbol of Christianity. The main hall is 30 m (98 ft) high and offers seating for 1120 people.

facts.fact: Slip forming, then used for grain elevators, earned it the nickname "Silo of the Souls".
facts.quote: Because at the time many grain elevators in Finland were built with slip forming, the church got the nicknames “Silo of the Souls” and “Viljanen’s Silo” (referring to the Vicar Paavo Viljanen).

facts.fact: All the furnishings are lacquered Finnish pine.
facts.quote: All furnishings in the church are made of lacquered Finnish pine.

facts.fact: It is a key work of post-war Finnish modernism, protected by the Church Act in 2006.
facts.quote: The church is considered to be among the key works of post-war Finnish modernism and was protected by the Church Act in 2006.

facts.fact: Oodi is a public library in central Helsinki, near the Central Station, the Music Centre and Kiasma.
facts.quote: The Helsinki Central Library Oodi (Finnish: Helsingin keskustakirjasto Oodi; Swedish: Helsingfors centrumbibliotek Ode), commonly referred to as Oodi (lit. 'ode'), is a public library in Helsinki, Finland. The library is situated in the Kluuvi district, close to Helsinki Central Station and next to Helsinki Music Centre and Kiasma Museum of Contemporary Art.

facts.fact: ALA Architects won the 2012 design competition against 543 other entries, with structural design by Ramboll Finland.
facts.quote: A design competition in 2012 to build the library was won by the Finnish architectural firm ALA Architects and structural design by Ramboll Finland. ALA Architects won the commission over 543 other competitors.

facts.fact: It opened on 5 December 2018, the eve of Finnish Independence Day.
facts.quote: The library was built in the Töölönlahti district next to Helsinki Music Centre and Kiasma Museum of Contemporary Art and inaugurated on 5 December 2018 on the eve of the Finnish Independence Day.

facts.fact: Robots carry returned books to the third floor, called Book Heaven, which holds about 100,000 books.
facts.quote: Specially designed robots transport returned books to the automated shelving system on the third floor, known as the Book Heaven, which houses around 100,000 books, alongside magazines, newspapers, films, sheet music and games.

facts.fact: The second floor is mainly for work, learning and making.
facts.quote: The second floor is dedicated primarily to work, learning and creative activities.

facts.fact: The building uses local materials and passive solar design and uses almost no energy.
facts.quote: The building is regarded as very energy-efficient due to its use of local materials and its use of sunlight. The building uses passive solar building design and uses almost no energy.

facts.fact: In 2019 IFLA named Oodi Public Library of the Year.
facts.quote: In 2019, the International Federation of Library Associations (IFLA) named Oodi as the best Public Library of the Year.

facts.fact: Oodi has a monumental inclined wooden wall forming an overhang, described as an ALA trademark.
facts.quote: Both Kilden and Oodi feature a monumental inclined wooden wall forming an overhang, which has been described as a trademark of ALA.

facts.fact: The Kursaal in San Sebastián, designed by Rafael Moneo and opened in 1999, holds a 1,800-seat auditorium plus multi-use and exhibition halls.
facts.quote: The Kursaal Congress Centre and Auditorium (Basque: Kursaal jauregia, Spanish: Palacio de Congresos y Auditorio Kursaal) is a multi-purpose exhibition complex located in Donostia-San Sebastián, Basque Country, Spain. Opened in 1999 and designed by Spanish architect Rafael Moneo, it consists of several spaces, including a 1,800-seat auditorium, multi-use and exhibition halls.

facts.fact: It is home to the San Sebastián International Film Festival.
facts.quote: The centre is the home to the largest film festival in Spain, the San Sebastian International Film Festival, founded in 1953.

facts.fact: In 2001 the building and Moneo won the European Union Prize for Contemporary Architecture.
facts.quote: In 2001, Kursaal Congress Centre and its architect Rafael Moneo were awarded the European Union Prize for Contemporary Architecture.

facts.fact: Moneo's scheme "Two Stranded Rocks" was chosen over designs by Botta, Foster, Isozaki and others in 1989.
facts.quote: In 1989, six internationally renowned architects were invited to a technical consultation: Mario Botta, Norman Foster, Arata Isozaki, Rafael Moneo, Juan Navarro Baldeweg and Luis Peña Ganchegui. Of the six projects, the one by Moneo, titled "Two Stranded Rocks" was chosen.

facts.fact: It is two large prisms rising from a platform, each an inner structure wrapped in double translucent glass panels on a metal frame.
facts.quote: It is mainly constituted as two large prismatic volumes, that emerge from a platform. Each "cube" (as they are known), is formed by an inner prismatic structure, surrounded by double translucent glass panels, which are supported by a metallic structure.

facts.fact: A large terrace between the two cubes looks out over Zurriola Beach and the mouth of the Urumea.
facts.quote: Between the cubes there is a large terrace, commanding views which take in the Zurriola Beach and the mouth of the Urumea river.

facts.fact: The main auditorium, in the bigger cube nearest the sea, seats 1,806.
facts.quote: Placed inside the biggest cube (and closest to the sea), this auditorium can hold an audience of 1,806, and is the most frequently used one for big events.

facts.fact: At first its impact on San Sebastián's classical French-style townscape was seen as negative.
facts.quote: Initially, the impact on the urban landscape of San Sebastian, dominated by its classical French-style architecture, was characterized as negative.

facts.fact: One of the first prominent postmodern works, the house in Chestnut Hill, Philadelphia, was designed by Robert Venturi for his mother and built 1962–1964.
facts.quote: The Vanna Venturi House, one of the first prominent works of the postmodern architecture movement, is located in the neighborhood of Chestnut Hill in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania.  It was designed by architect Robert Venturi for his mother, Vanna Venturi, and built between 1962 and 1964.

facts.fact: The five-room house is only about 30 feet tall, but its front reads as monumental through deliberate play with elements that signal scale.
facts.quote: The five-room house stands only about 30 feet (9 m) tall, but has a monumental front facade, an effect achieved by intentionally manipulating the architectural elements that indicate a building's scale.

facts.fact: A non-structural applied arch and "hole in the wall" windows openly challenged Modernist orthodoxy.
facts.quote: Elements such as a non-structural applique arch and "hole in the wall" windows were an open challenge to Modernist orthodoxy, as described in Venturi's 1966 book Complexity and Contradiction in Architecture .

facts.fact: Vincent Scully called it "the biggest small building of the second half of the twentieth century."
facts.quote: Architectural historian Vincent Scully called it "the biggest small building of the second half of the twentieth century."

facts.fact: Venturi designed it while writing Complexity and Contradiction in Architecture.
facts.quote: Venturi designed the Vanna Venturi House at the same time that he wrote his anti-Modernist polemic Complexity and Contradiction in Architecture in which he outlined his own architectural ideas.

facts.fact: Its pitched roof, central hearth and chimney, and closed ground floor react against Modernist elements.
facts.quote: Many of the basic elements of the house are a reaction against standard Modernist architectural elements: the pitched roof rather than flat roof, the emphasis on the central hearth and chimney, a closed ground floor "set firmly on the ground" rather than the Modernist columns and glass walls which open up the ground floor.

facts.fact: Vanna needed her whole daily routine on one floor, so the main rooms are all on the first floor.
facts.quote: As a widow nearing the age of 70 as the house was completed, Vanna required that all her daily routine could be conducted on one floor, possibly with the help of a live-in caretaker.  Thus the first floor plan contains all the main rooms of the house: the master bedroom, a full bathroom, the caretaker's room, the kitchen and a living/dining area.

facts.fact: The central chimney and staircase dominate the interior.
facts.quote: The central chimney and staircase dominate the interior of the house.

facts.fact: The New Museum of Contemporary Art in New York is among SANAA's notable works.
facts.quote: Notable works include the Toledo Museum of Art's Glass Pavilion in Toledo, Ohio; Grace Farms in New Canaan, Connecticut; the New Museum of Contemporary Art in New York; the Rolex Learning Center at the EPFL in Lausanne; the Serpentine Pavilion in London; the Christian Dior Building in Omotesandō, Tokyo; the 21st Century Museum of Contemporary Art in Kanazawa; the Louvre-Lens Museum in France; and the Bocconi New Campus in Milan.

facts.fact: The Portland Building is a 15-storey municipal office building in downtown Portland, opened in 1982.
facts.quote: The Portland Building, alternatively referenced as the Portland Municipal Services Building, is a 15-story municipal office building located at 1120 SW 5th Avenue in downtown Portland, Oregon. Built at a cost of US$29 million, it opened in 1982 and was considered architecturally groundbreaking at the time.

facts.fact: Michael Graves' mix of surface materials and colours, small windows and decorative flourishes made it an icon of postmodern architecture.
facts.quote: The distinctive look of Michael Graves' Portland Building, with its use of a variety of surface materials and colors, small windows, and inclusion of prominent decorative flourishes, was in stark contrast to the architectural style most commonly used for large office buildings at the time, and made the building an icon of postmodern architecture.

facts.fact: It was the first major postmodern tall office building, opening before Philip Johnson's AT&T Building.
facts.quote: It is the first major postmodern tall office building, opening before Philip Johnson's AT&T Building, and its design has been described as a rejection of the Modernist principles established in the early 20th century.

facts.fact: Graves won a large design competition; Philip Johnson sat on the selection committee.
facts.quote: Graves' design was selected in a large design competition, with Johnson as one of the three members of the selection committee.

facts.fact: The hammered-copper statue Portlandia was added above the entrance in 1985.
facts.quote: In 1985, the hammered-copper statue Portlandia was added above the front entrance.

facts.fact: It houses City of Portland offices next to City Hall and was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 2011.
facts.quote: The building houses offices of the City of Portland and is located adjacent to Portland City Hall.  It was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 2011.

facts.fact: In a 2017–2020 reconstruction a new unitized curtain wall followed Graves's design while fixing years of water damage.
facts.quote: The building envelope was replaced using a unitized curtain wall, allowing the design to reflect Graves's original while repairing years of moisture seeping into the facade and preventing further water damage.

facts.fact: It won an American Institute of Architects honor award in May 1983.
facts.quote: In May 1983, the building won an American Institute of Architects honor award.

facts.fact: The library in Vyborg was designed by Aino and Alvar Aalto and built 1927–1935, when the city was Finnish Viipuri.
facts.quote: Vyborg Library (Finnish: Viipurin kaupunginkirjasto) is a public library in Vyborg, Russia, designed by Finnish architects Aino Aalto and Alvar Aalto, built between 1927 and 1935 when the city (then named Viipuri) was part of Finland.

facts.fact: It is a pioneering functionalist masterpiece, acclaimed for its natural lighting, undulating timber auditorium ceiling and child-scaled interiors.
facts.quote: It is widely recognised as a pioneering masterpiece of 20th-century functionalist architecture and an early landmark of regional modernism. The building became internationally acclaimed for its innovative natural lighting systems, an undulating timber auditorium ceiling engineered for acoustic precision, and its custom child-scaled interior design.

facts.fact: The 1927 competition entry was Nordic Classicist; over 1928–1933 the design shifted to purist modernism.
facts.quote: Their original proposal reflected Nordic Classicism (influenced by Gunnar Asplund's Stockholm City Library), but over an extended five-year development phase from 1928 to 1933, the design shifted completely into a purist modernist style.

facts.fact: A stepped, sunken reading hall is lit by deep cylindrical skylights that spread daylight evenly without glare.
facts.quote:
Sunken reading well: A stepped central reading and lending hall that created an open, multi-level space.
Diffuse natural lighting: Deep cylindrical skylights designed to spread daylight evenly across reading desks without harsh glare.

facts.fact: The auditorium ceiling undulates in waves of red-hearted pine.
facts.quote: His Vyborg Library, built in what was then Viipuri (it became Vyborg after Soviet annexation in 1944), is acclaimed for its stunning ceiling, with its undulating waves of red-hearted pine (which grows in the region ).

facts.fact: It was Finland's first public library with a children's wing, whose interiors Aino Aalto led.
facts.quote: The library was the first public library in Finland to feature a dedicated children's wing and an open-shelf lending system. Aino Aalto led the child-scaled interior architecture and furniture design for this section.

facts.fact: After war damage and a decade of abandonment, the wave ceiling was completely destroyed.
facts.quote: The building suffered military damage and sat abandoned for a decade, leading to severe decay, including the total destruction of the auditorium's wave ceiling.

facts.fact: A restoration costing nearly 9 million euros was completed in late 2013.
facts.quote: The total restoration cost nearly 9 million euros and was completed in late 2013.

facts.fact: Marina City is a mixed-use residential and commercial complex in Chicago designed by Bertrand Goldberg.
facts.quote: Marina City is a mixed-use residential-commercial building complex in Chicago, Illinois, United States, designed by architect Bertrand Goldberg.

facts.fact: It has two 587-foot, 65-storey apartment towers, opened in 1963.
facts.quote: The complex consists of two 587-foot (179 m), 65-story apartment towers, opened in 1963, which include physical plant penthouses.

facts.fact: A small marina at river level beneath the platform gives the complex its name.
facts.quote: Beneath the platform, at river level, is a small marina for pleasure craft, giving the structures their name.

facts.fact: When finished, the towers were the world's tallest residential buildings and tallest reinforced concrete structures, built as a "city within a city".
facts.quote: When finished, the two towers were both the tallest residential buildings and the tallest reinforced concrete structures in the world. The complex was built as a "city within a city", featuring numerous on-site facilities including a theater, gym, swimming pool, ice rink, bowling alley, stores, restaurants, and its namesake marina.

facts.fact: The bottom 19 floors are an exposed spiral parking ramp.
facts.quote: The bottom 19 floors form an exposed spiral parking ramp operated by valet with approximately 896 parking spaces.

facts.fact: On each floor a circular hallway rings the 32-foot elevator core, with 16 wedge-shaped units around it.
facts.quote: On each residential floor, a circular hallway surrounds the elevator core, which is 32 feet (9.8 m) in diameter, with 16 sector-shaped units arrayed around the hallway.

facts.fact: Each unit ends in a semi-circular balcony, so every living room and bedroom has one.
facts.quote: Each unit terminates in a 175-square-foot (16.3 m2) semi-circular balcony, separated from living areas by a floor-to-ceiling window wall. Because of this arrangement, every single living room and bedroom in Marina City has a balcony.

facts.fact: It is credited with beginning the residential renaissance of American inner cities.
facts.quote: Marina City was one of the first major post-war urban high-rise residential complexes in the United States, and is widely credited with beginning the residential renaissance of American inner cities.

facts.fact: The National Taichung Theater is an opera house in Taichung, Taiwan.
facts.quote: The National Taichung Theater (Chinese: 臺中國家歌劇院; pinyin: Táizhōng Guójiā Gējù Yuàn; Pe̍h-ōe-jī: Tâi-Tiong Kok-Ka Koa-Ke̍k-Īⁿ) is an opera house in the Taichung's 7th Redevelopment Zone in the Xitun District of Taichung, Taiwan.

facts.fact: The building covers an estimated 57,685 square metres.
facts.quote: The estimated area of the structure is 57,685 square meters (620,920 sq ft).

facts.fact: It was designed by Toyo Ito with Cecil Balmond at Arup AGU.
facts.quote: It was designed by Japanese architect Toyo Ito in collaboration with Cecil Balmond at Arup AGU.

facts.fact: Toyo Ito won first prize in the Taichung Opera International Competition in 2006.
facts.quote: 2006 – First Prize "Taichung Opera International Competition" in Taiwan

facts.fact: It partly opened on 23 November 2014 and officially opened in 2016.
facts.quote: The venue had a partial opening on 23 November 2014. It was officially opened in 2016.

facts.fact: The Fondation Maeght is a modern art museum on a hill above Saint-Paul de Vence, founded by Marguerite and Aimé Maeght in 1964.
facts.quote: The Maeght Foundation or Fondation Maeght (pronounced [mɑɡ]) is a museum of modern art on the Colline des Gardettes, a hill overlooking Saint-Paul de Vence in the southeast of France about 25 km (16 mi) from Nice. It was established by Marguerite and Aimé Maeght in 1964 and houses paintings, sculptures, collages, ceramics and all forms of modern art.

facts.fact: Josep Lluís Sert, recommended by Joan Miró, designed it; the first idea was an artists' village, not a museum.
facts.quote: The building housing the foundation’s collections was designed by Catalan architect Josep Lluís Sert, recommended by Joan Miró. The initial idea was to create an artists’ village, not a museum.

facts.fact: Sert based the plan on a Mediterranean village, organised around the chapel.
facts.quote: Sert based his design on that of a Mediterranean village, with everything organized around a central point: the chapel.

facts.fact: Sert kept the natural slope, setting rooms, patios and gardens on terraces at different levels.
facts.quote: Sert retained the natural slope of the land, arranging exhibition rooms, patios, and gardens on various terrace levels, which gives the building its distinctive character.

facts.fact: Semi-vaulted roofs act as "light traps" that capture and diffuse sunlight into the galleries.
facts.quote: The issue of exhibition hall lighting was addressed by using semi-vaulted roofs, actual “light traps” that capture and diffuse sunlight through glass panels.

facts.fact: Two large white impluvia collect rainwater for the pools and shade the galleries to keep them cool.
facts.quote: The foundation’s two large white impluvium are iconic. They serve dual purposes: collecting rainwater to fill pools and providing coolness to the exhibition rooms through the shade they cast.

facts.fact: Artists including Giacometti, Miró, Chagall and Braque made works built into the architecture and gardens.
facts.quote: Painters and sculptors collaborated with Josep Lluís Sert on the architecture by creating works integrated into the building and nature: the Giacometti courtyard, the Miró Labyrinth filled with sculptures and ceramics, wall mosaics by Marc Chagall and Pierre Tal Coat, the pool and mosaic by Braque, the chapel's stained glass window based on the Birds theme created by Georges Braque for the ceiling of the Louvre museum, and Pol Bury's animated fountain.

facts.fact: France's Ministry of Culture has labelled the building "20th Century Heritage".
facts.quote: The building has been labeled as “20th Century Heritage” by the Ministry of Culture.

facts.fact: Villa Müller is a Modernist villa in Prague built in 1930, designed by Adolf Loos for František Müller.
facts.quote: The Villa Müller (Czech: Müllerova vila) is a Modernist villa in Prague, Czech Republic built in 1930. It was designed by Adolf Loos as a residence for František Müller, co-owner of the Kapsa-Müller construction company from Plzeň.

facts.fact: Müller's company specialised in reinforced concrete.
facts.quote: Mr. Müller was an engineer and co-owned a construction company called Kapsa and Müller. The company specialized in reinforced concrete, developing new construction techniques.

facts.fact: Architect Karel Lhota introduced Müller to Loos and contributed to the design because of Loos' poor health.
facts.quote: Soon, the architect Karel Lhota set František Müller up with Loos to design the villa. Lhota also contributed to the design due to Loos' poor health.

facts.fact: Its Raumplan shows in the different levels of rooms, which signal their function and importance.
facts.quote: The spatial design, known as Raumplan, is evident in the multi-level parts of individual rooms, indicating their function and symbolic importance. Raumplan is exhibited in the interior as well as the exterior.

facts.fact: Loos gave the villa a white, cubic facade.
facts.quote: For the exterior of the Villa Müller, Loos designed a white, cubic facade.

facts.fact: Loos set the public outside against a private inside richly finished in marble, wood and silk.
facts.quote: He also wanted to distinguish between the outside, where the view could be seen by the public eye, and the inside, the private spaces of those who lived there. Consequently, the interior is lavishly decorated with comfortable furniture and marble, wood, and silk surfaces.

facts.fact: Villa Müller is the example of Loos' Raumplan method of arranging interior spaces.
facts.quote: Loos became a pioneer of modern architecture and contributed a body of theory and criticism of Modernism in architecture and design and developed the "Raumplan" (literally spatial plan) method of arranging interior spaces, exemplified in Villa Müller in Prague.

facts.fact: The house was restored in 1998 and reopened as a museum in 2000.
facts.quote: The house was restored in 1998 and finally re-opened as a museum in 2000.

facts.fact: Siza worked with Eduardo Souto de Moura on Portugal's flagship pavilion at Expo '98 in Lisbon.
facts.quote: Another architect he has collaborated with is Eduardo Souto de Moura, e.g. on Portugal's flagship pavilions at Expo '98 in Lisbon and Expo 2000 in Hannover, as well as on the Serpentine Pavillon 2005.

facts.fact: The Pavilion of Portugal at Expo '98 in Lisbon dates from 1998.
facts.quote: 1998: Pavilion of Portugal in Expo'98, Lisbon, Portugal.

facts.fact: VM Houses are two apartment buildings in Ørestad, Copenhagen; the M House was completed in 2004 and the V House in 2005.
facts.quote: VM Houses is a housing project consisting of two adjacent apartment buildings in  Ørestad, Copenhagen, Denmark. Designed by JDS Architects and Bjarke Ingels Group, the M House with 95 units was completed in 2004 and the V House with 114 units, in 2005.

facts.fact: Developer Per Høpfner commissioned PLOT, the firm of Bjarke Ingels and Julien De Smedt, though they had never built at this scale.
facts.quote: The developer Per Høpfner, working with the Dansk Olie og Naturgas company -now DONG Energy-, was interested in creating housing in Ørestad on land purchased from the state. Despite the fact that Bjarke Ingels and Julien De Smedt had not built anything on such a large scale before, he decided to commission PLOT, their architecture firm, to design VM Houses.

facts.fact: Inspired by Le Corbusier's Unité d'Habitation, the two blocks are shaped like the letters V and M for daylight, privacy and views.
facts.quote: Inspired by Le Corbusier's Unité d'Habitation concept, two residential blocks, with footprints in the shape of the letters V and M, have been designed with an emphasis on daylight, privacy and views.

facts.fact: Every apartment has diagonal views of the landscape instead of the neighbouring block, and corridors are short.
facts.quote: Rather than looking over the neighbouring building, all the apartments have diagonal views of the surrounding landscape. Corridors are short, rather like bullet holes through the building.

facts.fact: There are some 80 different apartment types.
facts.quote: There are some 80 different types of apartment in the complex, adaptable to individual needs.

facts.fact: The developer said it came in on budget.
facts.quote: "VM may look crazy," Høpfner remarked, "but it came in on budget."

facts.fact: It was De Smedt and Ingels' first major project and won the Forum AID Award for best building in Scandinavia in 2006.
facts.quote: VM Houses was the first major project to be designed by Julien De Smedt and Bjarke Ingels, winning them the Forum AID Award for the best building in Scandinavia in 2006.

facts.fact: Villa Cavrois in Croix is a large modernist mansion built in 1932 by Robert Mallet-Stevens for the textile industrialist Paul Cavrois.
facts.quote: Villa Cavrois in Croix is a large modernist mansion built in 1932 by French architect Robert Mallet-Stevens for Paul Cavrois, an industrialist from Roubaix active in the textile industry.

facts.fact: Given free rein, Mallet-Stevens designed everything down to the last detail, as a total work of art.
facts.quote: The owners gave the architect free rein on the project, and, for the first time in his career, Mallet-Stevens was responsible for the entire work, down to the last details. The villa is conceived by the architect as a total artwork and it represents the outcome of his technical and aesthetic reflections.

facts.fact: The brief, commissioned in 1929, was "air, light, work, sports, hygiene, comfort and efficiency".
facts.quote: Clear guidelines governed the design of the building, which was commissioned in 1929, included: "air, light, work, sports, hygiene, comfort and efficiency".

facts.fact: The villa is 60 metres long, with 830 m² of terraces.
facts.quote: The villa is 60 meters long, it has 3800 m2 including 1840 m2 habitables and 830 m2 of terraces and a garden of 17600 m2 (originally 5 ha).

facts.fact: Its yellow bricks, made in 26 mould shapes, were inspired by Dudok's Hilversum town hall.
facts.quote: The French firm Bonzel produced twenty-six moulds of different form in order to make bricks capables to cover the diverse areas of the villa. The source of inspiration of this brick is the town hall of Hilversum, in the Netherlands, realized by the architect Willem Marinus Dudok.

facts.fact: Its look is modern, but its plan follows French châteaux: two symmetrical wings around a central vestibule and hall.
facts.quote: If the aesthetic canon of the villa is resolutely modern (large glass windows, flat-roofs, total absence of decoration, purity of lines), its plan is in line with the French tradition of the 17th- and 18-century châteaux: two symmetrical wings (the parents' wing and the children and household staff wing) evolve around the central corp of the villa, constituted by the vestibule and the hall salon.

facts.fact: The property was classified as a historic monument in 1990.
facts.quote: In 1990, the property and grounds were classified as an historic monument by decree of the Conseil d'État.

facts.fact: The French state bought it in 2001 and began restoring it in 2004.
facts.quote: The French State, through its Ministry of Culture, purchased the building in 2001, and, in 2004, restoration work commenced on the exterior and the reinstatement of the internal features.

facts.fact: Stockholm Public Library was designed by Gunnar Asplund and is one of the city's most notable buildings.
facts.quote: Stockholm Public Library (Swedish: Stockholms stadsbibliotek or Stadsbiblioteket) is a library building in Stockholm, Sweden, designed by Swedish architect Gunnar Asplund, and one of the city's most notable structures.

facts.fact: A design was proposed in 1922 and construction began in 1924.
facts.quote: Discussed by a committee of which Asplund himself was a member from 1918, a design scheme was proposed in 1922, and construction began in 1924.

facts.fact: Partly inspired by Ledoux's Rotonde de la Villette, Asplund dropped a dome for a tall cylindrical rotunda.
facts.quote: Partly inspired by the Barrière Saint-Martin (Rotonde de la Villette) by Claude Nicolas Ledoux, Asplund abandoned earlier ideas for a dome in favour of a rotunda whose tall cylinder gives the exterior some monumentality.

facts.fact: He reduced the classical order to abstract geometric forms, mostly removing decoration.
facts.quote: In the course of its planning, he reduced elements of the classical order to their most abstract geometrical forms, for the most part eliminating architectural decor.

facts.fact: It was Sweden's first public library with open shelves, an idea Asplund studied in the United States.
facts.quote: Stockholm Public Library was Sweden's first public library to apply the principle of open shelves where visitors could access books without the need to ask library staff for assistance, a concept Asplund studied in the United States during the construction of the library.

facts.fact: It opened on 31 March 1928; the west wing completing the square base around the rotunda came in 1932.
facts.quote: Officially opened on 31 March 1928 in the presence of Prince Eugen, due to financial constraints the library was still missing its west wing which was only added in 1932 to complete the approximately square base around the rotunda of the main reading room.

facts.fact: It shows Asplund's gradual shift from classicism to functionalism.
facts.quote: Stockholm Public Library is one of Asplund's most important works and illustrates his gradual shift from classicism to functionalism.

facts.fact: It is the prototypical example of Nordic Classicism, or Swedish Grace.
facts.quote: Among Asplund's most important works is the Stockholm Public Library, constructed between 1924 and 1928, which stands as the prototypical example of the Nordic Classicism and so-called Swedish Grace movement.

facts.fact: Mountain Dwellings in Ørestad, Copenhagen, places apartments above a multi-storey car park; it was designed by PLOT (BIG+JDSA).
facts.quote: Mountain Dwellings (Danish: Bjerget) is a building in the Ørestad district of  Copenhagen, Denmark, consisting of apartments above a multi-story car park. The building was designed by the Danish architectural practice PLOT (BIG+JDSA).

facts.fact: The flats climb the garage's sloping roof up to the 11th floor as a south-facing "mountainside", each with a backyard on the roof of the flat below.
facts.quote: The apartments scale the diagonally sloping roof of the parking garage, from street level to 11th floor, creating an artificial, south facing 'mountainside'. Each apartment has a "backyard" on the roof of the property in front and below it.

facts.fact: The garage holds 480 cars.
facts.quote: The parking garage contains parking spots for 480 cars.

facts.fact: Under the flats, the garage ceilings are painted in Verner Panton's colours, running from green for earth to blue for sky.
facts.quote: The space has up to 16 m high ceilings, and the underside of each level of apartments is covered in aluminum painted in a distinctive colour scheme of psychedelic hues which, as a tribute to Danish 1960s and '70s furniture designer Verner Panton, are all exact matches of the colours he used in his designs. The colours move, symbolically, from green for the earth over yellow, orange, dark orange, hot pink, purple to bright blue for the sky.

facts.fact: The slope carries 80 penthouses, each L-shaped with a terrace and small garden.
facts.quote: The sloping roof is covered with a single layer of 80 penthouses. Each apartment has an L-shaped floor plan and a terrace and small garden outside, located on the roof of the in-front, lower-level apartment.

facts.fact: The L-plan with a small courtyard was inspired by Jørn Utzon's Kingo Houses.
facts.quote: The L-shape floor plan in combination with a small courtyard was inspired by Jørn Utzon's Kingo Houses north of Copenhagen.

facts.fact: Perforated aluminium plates ventilate and light the garage, and their holes form a giant image of Mount Everest.
facts.quote: The parking garage is protected from wind and rain by huge shiny aluminium plates, perforated to let in light and allow for natural ventilation. By controlling the size of the holes, the sheeting was transformed into the giant rasterized image of Mount Everest.

facts.fact: It won the 2008 World Architecture Festival Award for Best Residential Building.
facts.quote: 2008 World Architecture Festival Award for Best Residential Building

facts.fact: The Met is a 66-storey condominium on Sathorn Road in Bangkok; in 2012 it was Thailand's tallest condominium.
facts.quote: The Met is a 66-story condominium located in Bangkok on Sathorn Road. As of 2012, it was the tallest condominium in Thailand and fourth-tallest building in Bangkok.

facts.fact: It is 228 metres tall, with 370 units in six towers linked by sky bridges.
facts.quote: The Met has a height of 228 metres and 66 floors. It contains 370 condominium units. It is composed of six towers connected by sky bridges.

facts.fact: Sunshades, overhangs and green walls shade the interiors, and the gaps between towers hold terraces, pools and sky gardens.
facts.quote: Sunshades, overhangs, and walls of live greenery filter sunlight and protect interiors from overheating. The gaps between the towers contain terraces with pools and sky gardens.

facts.fact: Openings through the building strengthen passing breezes; it was conceived as a model tower for a low-wind tropical climate.
facts.quote: The apertures through this building are meant to increase the strength of passing breezes and to cool the living units. The architects conceived of this building as a model for high-rise construction in a low-wind tropical climate, reworking the worldwide model developed for cold climates with high winds.

facts.fact: Every unit is cross-ventilated, so residents can live without air conditioning.
facts.quote: All units are cross-ventilated, leaving residents a viable option to not use air conditioning.

facts.fact: WOHA completed The Met in 2009.
facts.quote: In 2009, the firm completed the School of the Arts campus in Singapore and The Met residential tower in Bangkok.

facts.fact: It won the 2010 International Highrise Award, cited for tropical living without air conditioning.
facts.quote: In 2010, the Met won the German Architecture Museum's International Highrise Award and was cited for "sustainable living conditions in this tropical region without recourse to air conditioning".

facts.fact: It won the RIBA Lubetkin Prize in 2011.
facts.quote: The building was the RIBA 2011 Lubetkin Prize winner.

facts.fact: The house in Palm Springs was designed by Richard Neutra in 1946 for Edgar J. Kaufmann, Sr., who also commissioned Fallingwater.
facts.quote: The Kaufmann Desert House, or simply the Kaufmann House, is a house in Palm Springs, California, that was designed by architect Richard Neutra in 1946. It was commissioned by Edgar J. Kaufmann, Sr., a businessman who also commissioned Fallingwater by Frank Lloyd Wright.

facts.fact: It was a desert retreat from harsh winters, made famous by Julius Shulman's 1947 photographs.
facts.quote: The house was commissioned by Edgar J. Kaufmann, Sr., the owner of Kaufmann's Department Store in Pittsburgh, as a desert retreat from harsh winters. It was made famous by photographs taken by Julius Shulman in 1947 and the 1970 photograph "Poolside Gossip" by Slim Aarons.

facts.fact: It has been called "an architectural marvel that helped define the modernist aesthetic" of Palm Springs.
facts.quote: The house has been described as "an architectural marvel that helped define the modernist aesthetic of the resort city of Palm Springs".

facts.fact: It is a Class 1 Historic Site of Palm Springs.
facts.quote: It is designated a Class 1 Historic Site by Palm Springs City Council.

facts.fact: Marmol Radziner + Associates restored it to its original design in a five-year project begun in 1993.
facts.quote: Seeking to restore the home to its original design, the Harrises contacted Marmol Radziner + Associates to undertake the five-year project, which began in 1993.

facts.fact: A closed section of a Utah quarry was reopened to supply matching stone.
facts.quote: The Harrises were also able to have a long-closed section of a Utah quarry reopened to mine matching stone to replace what had been removed or damaged.

facts.fact: Adjoining plots were bought to restore the desert buffer Neutra had envisioned around the 3,200 sq ft house.
facts.quote: To help restore the desert buffer Neutra had envisioned for the house, the Harrises also bought several adjoining plots to more than double the land around the 3,200-square-foot (300 m2) house.

facts.fact: A 2008 Los Angeles Times survey of experts put it among the all-time top 10 houses in Los Angeles.
facts.quote: The Kaufmann house was included in a list of all-time top 10 houses in Los Angeles, despite its location in Palm Springs, in a Los Angeles Times survey of experts in December 2008.

facts.fact: Kirche am Steinhof is the church of the Otto-Wagner-Spital in Vienna, designed by Otto Wagner, and one of the most important Art Nouveau churches.
facts.quote: Kirche am Steinhof, also called the Church of St. Leopold, is the Roman Catholic oratory of the Otto-Wagner-Spital in the area of Steinhof in Vienna, Austria. The building, designed by Otto Wagner, is considered one of the most important Art Nouveau churches in the world.

facts.fact: Wagner built it 1903–1907, with mosaics and stained glass by Koloman Moser and angels by Othmar Schimkowitz.
facts.quote: The church dedicated to Saint Leopold was built between 1903 and 1907 by the 63-year-old architect Otto Wagner, with mosaics and stained glass by Koloman Moser and sculptural angels by Othmar Schimkowitz (1864–1947).

facts.fact: It sits on a north–south axis at the top centre of the hospital complex.
facts.quote: Unusually the church lies on a north–south axis, at the centre-top of the hospital complex.

facts.fact: Wagner consulted doctors and nurses about the needs of a chapel for mentally ill patients.
