facts.quote: When drafting his plans for the building, the commissioned architect, Otto Wagner, respected the church's role as the institutional chapel for mentally ill patients and consulted with doctors and nurses concerning the specific requirements of such a building.

facts.fact: Features for the asylum include rounded corners, emergency exits in the side walls and separate entrances for men and women.
facts.quote: Otto Wagner incorporated numerous features specifically related to its function within an asylum: e.g. there are very few sharp edges, and most corners are rounded; almost no crosses are visible; the priest's area is potentially entirely separate from the patients'; access to the pulpit is only from the vestry; emergency exits are built into the side walls in case a patient needed to be speedily removed; continuously flowing water replaced holy water stoups at the entrance; there were separate entrances for male and female patients, since gender segregation was mandatory in mental institutions at the time; confessionals were more open than is customary.

facts.fact: The floor slopes about 26 cm from entrance to altar, like a theatre, for clearer views.
facts.quote: The floor is raked as in a theatre, though not as steeply; the fall from entrance to altar is approx. 26 centimetres (10 in): standing at the back the view to the altar is thus less obstructed.

facts.fact: The dome cannot be seen from inside; the nave has a six-second echo and seats 800.
facts.quote: The dome of the church is not visible from inside the building; even so, the nave has an echo of six seconds. The church seats 800 people when full.

facts.fact: Between 2002 and 2004 the 1,800 m² facade was re-clad with 3,000 Carrara marble plates.
facts.quote: Between 2002 and 2004, the entirety of the church's 1,800m² façade was replaced with 3000 plates of Carrara marble, each tile having been examined by ultrasound to ensure quality.

facts.fact: The Schindler House in West Hollywood was designed by Rudolph M. Schindler.
facts.quote: The Schindler House, also known as the Schindler Chace House or Kings Road House, is a house in West Hollywood, California, designed by architect Rudolph M. Schindler.

facts.fact: It has no conventional living room, dining room or bedrooms; it was a shared live/work space for two young families.
facts.quote: The Schindler House was a departure from existing residential architecture because of what it did not have; there is no conventional living room, dining room or bedrooms in the house. The residence was meant to be a cooperative live/work space for two young families.

facts.fact: Concrete walls and sliding canvas panels used industrial materials, and the open plan joined house and outdoors, a precedent for California.
facts.quote: The concrete walls and sliding canvas panels made novel use of industrial materials, while the open floor plan integrated the external environment into the residence, setting a precedent for California architecture in particular.

facts.fact: The concrete slab is both foundation and floor, and the walls are tilt-up concrete slabs cast on it.
facts.quote: The house is built on a flat concrete slab, which is both the foundation and the final floor. The walls are concrete tilt up slabs, poured into forms on top of the foundation.

facts.fact: The tilt-up slabs are 3 inches apart, the gaps filled with concrete, clear glass or frosted glass.
facts.quote: The tilt up slabs are separated by 3 inches (76 mm), filled with concrete, clear glass or frosted glass.

facts.fact: Built with Clyde Chace, it was started in November 1921 and completed by June 1922 for $12,550.
facts.quote: With Schindler as architect and Chace as builder to save costs, construction began in November 1921. Construction was complete by June 1922, with a total cost of $12,550.

facts.fact: It is laid out as two interlocking L-shaped apartments, based on a campsite Schindler had seen.
facts.quote: The Schindler House is laid out as two interlinking L-shaped apartments (referred to as the Schindler and Chace apartments) using the basic design of the camp site that he had seen a year before.

facts.fact: Instead of bedrooms there are two rooftop sleeping baskets.
facts.quote: Instead of bedrooms, there are two rooftop sleeping baskets.

facts.fact: The Torino Esposizioni complex, Turin's 1930s exhibition hall, has a main hall in reinforced concrete designed by Pier Luigi Nervi.
facts.quote: Other buildings in Corso Massimo d'Azeglio include the Torino Esposizioni complex (Turin's exhibition hall built in the 1930s) featuring a monumental entrance with a large full height porch, a main hall designed by Pier Luigi Nervi in reinforced concrete, and the Teatro Nuovo, a theatre mostly focused on ballet exhibitions.

facts.fact: The Maison de Verre (House of Glass) was built in Paris from 1928 to 1932.
facts.quote: The Maison de Verre (French for House of Glass) was built from 1928 to 1932 in Paris, France.

facts.fact: Its design stressed honesty of materials, variable transparency and industrial fittings set against traditional décor.
facts.quote: Constructed in the early modern style of architecture, the house's design emphasized three primary traits: honesty of materials, variable transparency of forms, and juxtaposition of "industrial" materials and fixtures with a more traditional style of home décor.

facts.fact: The main materials are steel, glass and glass block.
facts.quote: The primary materials used were steel, glass, and glass block.

facts.fact: It was designed by Pierre Chareau with architect Bernard Bijvoet and metalworker Louis Dalbet.
facts.quote: The design was a collaboration among Pierre Chareau (a furniture and interiors designer), Bernard Bijvoet (a Dutch architect working in Paris since 1927) and Louis Dalbet (craftsman metalworker).

facts.fact: Translucent glass block walls form the outside; inside, sliding, folding and rotating screens change the spaces.
facts.quote: The external form is defined by translucent glass block walls, with select areas of clear glazing for transparency. Internally, spatial division is variable by the use of sliding, folding or rotating screens in glass, sheet or perforated metal, or in combination.

facts.fact: The house included a ground-floor medical suite for Dr. Jean Dalsace.
facts.quote: The program of the home was somewhat unusual in that it included a ground-floor medical suite for Dr. Jean Dalsace.

facts.fact: A top-floor tenant refused to sell, so the lower three floors were demolished and the house built underneath that floor.
facts.quote: Much to his or her chagrin, however, the elderly tenant on the top floor of the building absolutely refused to sell, and so the patron was obliged to completely demolish the bottom three floors of the building and construct the Maison de Verre underneath, all without disturbing the original top floor.

facts.fact: It was the first house in France made of steel and glass.
facts.quote: Chareau designed the first house in France made of steel and glass, the Maison de Verre.

facts.fact: Hilversum Town Hall was designed by Willem Marinus Dudok as the seat of the municipal council and completed in 1931.
facts.quote: The Hilversum Town Hall (Dutch: Raadhuis Hilversum) was designed by Willem Marinus Dudok to serve as seat of the municipal council of Hilversum in the Netherlands. Construction was completed in 1931.

facts.fact: It is considered Dudok's finest work and one of the most influential buildings of its time.
facts.quote: It is a much-admired building that is considered the finest example of Dudok's work and internationally recognized as one of the most influential buildings of its time.

facts.fact: Dudok's 1924 design used an elevated site on the former Den Witten Hull estate northwest of the town centre.
facts.quote: Dudok presented the first sketches for a new design in 1924, for which he was able to use an elevated location on the former Den Witten Hull estate, which had been purchased by the municipality in 1923 to the northwest of the town centre.

facts.fact: Set in a park, the light-coloured building rises from water, expressing Hilversum's garden-city character.
facts.quote: It is surrounded by a park and the light-coloured building rises from water, highlighting the garden city character that Hilversum wanted to achieve.

facts.fact: The building is planned around two squares: a courtyard ringed by offices and a second courtyard crossed by a service road.
facts.quote: Somewhat reminiscent of the early designs of Frank Lloyd Wright, the Town Hall building consists of two squares; an inner courtyard surrounded by offices and a second courtyard surrounded by low spaces and traversed by a service road.

facts.fact: Its dramatic massing, asymmetry and overhanging eaves show the influence of Frank Lloyd Wright and the Prairie School.
facts.quote: While his early style in Hilversum grew out of the Amsterdam School, the dramatic massing, asymmetry, the overhanging eaves and other elements of his landmark Hilversum City Hall were clearly influenced by Frank Lloyd Wright and the Chicago Prairie School.

facts.fact: Its bell was broadcast every hour on public radio until the 1960s.
facts.quote: The sound of its bell was broadcast live every hour on public radio stations until the 1960s, reflecting the town's role as the principal media centre for the Netherlands.

facts.fact: During the 1989–1995 restoration, most of the soft, porous original bricks had frost damage and were largely replaced.
facts.quote: The building was restored between 1989 and 1995. Almost all of the original bricks, which had been baked too softly and were porous, had sustained frost damage.

facts.fact: Parliament House in Canberra is the meeting place of the Parliament of Australia.
facts.quote: Parliament House is the meeting place of the Parliament of Australia, the legislative branch of Australia's federal tier of government.

facts.fact: It was designed by Mitchell/Giurgola & Thorp Architects.
facts.quote: Parliament House was designed by Mitchell/Giurgola & Thorp Architects and constructed by a joint venture comprising Concrete Constructions and John Holland.

facts.fact: The design competition drew 329 entries from 29 countries.
facts.quote: The design competition drew 329 entries from 29 countries.

facts.fact: Mitchell/Giurgola won with a design that buried most of the building under Capital Hill, capped by a huge spire carrying the flag.
facts.quote: The competition winner was the Philadelphia-based architectural firm of Mitchell/Giurgola, with the on-site work directed by the Italian-born architect Romaldo Giurgola, with a design which involved burying most of the building under Capital Hill, and capping the edifice with an enormous spire topped by a large Australian flag.

facts.fact: The spires holding the flagpole trace the outline of the triangular capitol Walter Burley Griffin envisioned.
facts.quote: The spires supporting the flag pole traces the outline of the triangular capitol building envisioned by Griffin.

facts.fact: Two large curved walls divide the building into four quadrants: entrance, House of Representatives, executive wing and Senate.
facts.quote: The design of Parliament House is anchored around two large curved walls that divides the structure into four quadrants. Clockwise these are: the formal entrance and event space, the House of Representatives, the executive wing and the Senate.

facts.fact: The walls are sunk into the hill so the building seems to emerge from the land, and people can walk on the grass roofs above their representatives.
facts.quote: These walls are sunken into the hill so that the building appears to emerge from the land, rather that towering over those beneath it. The ability for people to walk on the grass roofs over their representatives also represents the people being above the government.

facts.fact: Elizabeth II opened it on 9 May 1988; it cost more than $1.1 billion.
facts.quote: The current Parliament House was officially opened on 9 May 1988 by Elizabeth II, Queen of Australia. It cost more than $1.1 billion (equivalent to about $2.6 billion in 2022) to build.

facts.fact: The 216.61 m Fernsehturm Stuttgart was the world's first telecommunications tower built of reinforced concrete, the original needle tower with a "basket" on top.
facts.quote: Fernsehturm Stuttgart (English: SWR TV Tower Stuttgart) is a 216.61 m (710.7 ft) telecommunications tower in Stuttgart, Germany. It was the world's first telecommunications tower constructed from reinforced concrete, and is thus the original modernist architecture highrise needle tower with a "basket" atop that would be built worldwide in the following years.

facts.fact: Controversial at first, it quickly became a landmark and tourist attraction.
facts.quote: Although controversial at first, it quickly became a well known landmark of Stuttgart and a tourist attraction.

facts.fact: It stands on the Hoher Bopser hill in Degerloch, southern Stuttgart.
facts.quote: The tower is located on the hill Hoher Bopser (elevation 483 meters) in the southern Stuttgart borough of Degerloch.

facts.fact: Critics objected to the new method and cost; construction began on 10 January 1954 and took 20 months.
facts.quote: The tower's construction was controversial – critics opposed the new building method and its costs; a simple 200-meter antenna array would have cost just 200,000 DM. Construction began on 10 January 1954 and continued for 20 months.

facts.fact: It cost 4.2 million DM, recovered from visitors within five years.
facts.quote: The construction cost was 4.2 million DM. Revenues from visitors reached that sum within five years.

facts.fact: It went into service on 5 February 1956.
facts.quote: The tower was placed in service on 5 February 1956 by Süddeutscher Rundfunk (today Südwestrundfunk – SWR).

facts.fact: The tower is among the major structures of engineer Fritz Leonhardt.
facts.quote: His major structures include the Cologne-Rodenkirchen Bridge, Stuttgart Television Tower, Hamburg's Alsterschwimmhalle and various cable-stayed bridges in Düsseldorf.

facts.fact: Its foundation is 27 m across.
facts.quote: Diameter of foundation: 27 m (89 ft)

facts.fact: MuCEM is a national ethnology museum in Marseille, built as part of the Euroméditerranée renewal opposite Fort Saint-Jean.
facts.quote: The Museum of European and Mediterranean Civilisations (Mucem or MuCEM; French: Musée des Civilisations de l'Europe et de la Méditerranée; Occitan: Museu de las Civilizacions Europèas e Mediterranèas) is an ethnology national museum in Marseille, France. It was built as part of the Euroméditerranée urban renewal project along with the neighbouring Villa Méditerranée in the La Joliette neighbourhood in the 2nd arrondissement opposite Fort Saint-Jean.

facts.fact: It opened in 2013, when Marseille was European Capital of Culture, and won the Council of Europe Museum Prize in 2015.
facts.quote: It was inaugurated in 2013 by President François Hollande as part of Marseille-Provence 2013, a year when Marseille was designated as the European Capital of Culture. In 2015, it won the Council of Europe Museum Prize.

facts.fact: It stands on reclaimed land at the harbour entrance, beside the 17th-century Fort Saint-Jean.
facts.quote: The museum is built on reclaimed land at the entrance to the harbour, next to the site of the 17th-century Fort Saint-Jean and a former port terminal called the J4.

facts.fact: A high footbridge, 130 m long, crosses the channel to Fort Saint-Jean.
facts.quote: A channel separates the new building and the Fort Saint-Jean, which has been restructured as part of the project. The two sites are linked by a high footbridge, 130 m (430 ft) long.

facts.fact: Rudy Ricciotti designed it with Roland Carta, built "of stone, water and wind".
facts.quote: The museum, built "of stone, water and wind", was designed by the architect Rudy Ricciotti in collaboration with the architect Roland Carta.

facts.fact: It is a 15,000 m² cube wrapped in a lattice shell of fibre-reinforced concrete, with an underground 400-seat auditorium.
facts.quote: A cube of 15,000 square metres (160,000 sq ft) surrounded by a latticework shell of fibre-reinforced concrete, it houses exhibits on two levels, with an underground auditorium seating 400.

facts.fact: A rooftop terrace restaurant looks over the bay of Marseille.
facts.quote: There is a restaurant on the terrace at the top of the building with panoramic views of the bay of Marseille, the Corniche and the Prado.

facts.fact: The final cost was €350 million against €160 million planned.
facts.quote: In February 2015, the French Court of Auditors ("la Cour des comptes") pointed out "a laborious gestation" with a final cost of €350 million (studies, construction...) instead of €160 million originally planned for the Musée des Civilisations de l'Europe et de la Méditerranée in Marseille.

facts.fact: The Shukhov Radio Tower in Moscow, designed by Vladimir Shukhov, is a 160 m free-standing steel diagrid structure built 1920–1922.
facts.quote: The Shukhov Radio Tower (Russian: Шуховская башня), also known as the Shabolovka Tower (Шаболовская башня), is a broadcasting tower deriving from the Russian avant-garde in Moscow designed by Vladimir Shukhov. The 160-metre-high (520 ft) free-standing steel diagrid structure was built between 1920 and 1922, during the Russian Civil War.

facts.fact: Shukhov sought strength and rigidity with as little material as possible.
facts.quote: He aimed not only to achieve greater strength and rigidity of the structure, but also ease and simplicity through the use of as little building material as possible.

facts.fact: A 350 m tower was planned, but war shortages cut it to 148.5 m and 240 tons.
facts.quote: The planned height of the new nine-sectioned hyperbolic tower was 350 metres (1,150 ft) (15 metres (49 ft) taller than the Eiffel Tower, which was taken into consideration when creating the plan) with an estimated mass of 2,200 tons (the Eiffel Tower weighs 7,300 tons). However, in the context of the Civil War and the lack of resources, the project had to be revised: the height was reduced to 148.5 metres (487 ft), the weight to 240 tons.

facts.fact: It was built with winches only, without cranes or scaffolding.
facts.quote: Tower construction was carried out without any cranes and scaffolding, but only with winches.

facts.fact: It has six stacked sections, each an independent hyperboloid on a larger one.
facts.quote: The tower is composed of six sections, one above the other. Each section is an independent hyperboloid based on a larger one.

facts.fact: Each section is a hyperboloid of straight beams whose ends rest on circular foundations.
facts.quote: The tower sections are single-cavity hyperboloids of rotation made of straight beams, the ends of which rest against circular foundations.

facts.fact: The diagrid steel shell takes minimal wind load.
facts.quote: The tower has a diagrid structure, and its steel shell experiences minimum wind load (a significant design factor for high-rising buildings).

facts.fact: After a campaign against demolition, Moscow placed a preservation order on it in September 2014.
facts.quote: Following a concerted campaign calling for the preservation of the tower, on July 3 the Ministry of Culture of Russia announced that the tower will not be demolished, and in September 2014 that Moscow City Council had placed a preservation order on the tower in order to safeguard it.

facts.fact: The Louisiana is Scandinavia's most visited museum of modern and contemporary art.
facts.quote: Attracting over 700,000 guests annually, the Louisiana is Scandinavia's most visited museum for modern and contemporary art, hosting 6 to 10 exhibitions each year alongside a permanent display of Yayoi Kusama's Gleaming Lights of the Souls.

facts.fact: It is on the Øresund coast, about 30 km north of central Copenhagen.
facts.quote: The museum is located by the Øresund coast in the North Zeeland region, some 30 km (19 mi) north of central Copenhagen and 10 km (6 mi) south of Elsinore.

facts.fact: It is a modernist landmark of Danish architecture, known for joining art, architecture and landscape.
facts.quote: The museum is recognized as a modernist landmark in Danish architecture, and is noted for its synthesis of art, architecture and landscape, boasting a sculpture park with works by Alexander Calder, Henry Moore and Richard Serra.

facts.fact: The name comes from Alexander Brun's three wives, all called Louise; Brun built the villa, now part of the museum, in 1855.
facts.quote: The name of the museum is derived from the first owner of the property, hofjægermester Alexander Brun, who named the estate after his three wives, all called Louise. Brun built the villa in which the part of the museum resides in 1855.

facts.fact: Architects Vilhelm Wohlert and Jørgen Bo walked the property for months; the first museum, opened in 1958, was three buildings linked by glass corridors.
facts.quote: In lieu of this, he partnered up with architects Vilhelm Wohlert and Jørgen Bo, who spent a few months walking around the property before deciding how a new construction would best fit into the landscape. This study resulted in the first version of the museum consisting of three buildings connected by glass corridors, which opened in conjunction with the museum as a whole, in 1958.

facts.fact: Wohlert and Bo worked on the museum for 33 years from 1958.
facts.quote: In 1958, he and his partner and fellow architect Jørgen Bo  (1919–1999) started work on the Danish modernist architecture Louisiana Museum of Modern Art  in Humlebæk,  a project on which they would work for the next 33 years.

facts.fact: A sculpture garden above the sea lies between the museum's two wings.
facts.quote: Perched above the sea, there is a sculpture garden between the museum's two wings with works by artists including Henry Moore, Alexander Calder, and Jean Arp.

facts.fact: Thorncrown Chapel in Eureka Springs, Arkansas, was designed by E. Fay Jones and built in 1980, recalling the Prairie School of his mentor Frank Lloyd Wright.
facts.quote: Thorncrown Chapel was designed by E. Fay Jones and constructed in Eureka Springs, Arkansas, in 1980. The design recalls the Prairie School of architecture popularized by Frank Lloyd Wright, with whom Jones had apprenticed.

facts.fact: Jim Reed commissioned it as a non-denominational chapel for meditation; the design was inspired by Sainte-Chapelle in Paris.
facts.quote: The chapel was commissioned by Jim Reed, a retired schoolteacher who envisioned a non-denominational pilgrimage chapel set apart for meditation. The design was inspired by Sainte-Chapelle, a Gothic church in Paris pierced by numerous stained glass windows.

facts.fact: It is 48 ft high, 24 ft wide and 60 ft long, with 425 windows totalling 6,000 sq ft of glass.
facts.quote: The chapel stands 48 feet (15 meters) high, 24 feet (7.3 meters) wide, and 60 feet (18 meters) long. It has 425 windows, which add up to 6,000 square feet (approximately 560 square meters) of glass.

facts.fact: To protect the site, no structural piece could be larger than two men could carry through the woods.
facts.quote: During the design process, Jones decided that in order to preserve the site's natural setting, no structural element could be larger than what two men could carry through the woods.

facts.fact: It is built of local materials: pressure-treated Southern pine, with flagstone floor and wall.
facts.quote: The structure was constructed using organic materials indigenous to northwestern Arkansas, including pressure-treated Southern pine and flagstone for the floor and surrounding wall.

facts.fact: It looks open-air but is an enclosed, air-conditioned space seating 100.
facts.quote: The chapel looks like an open-air structure, but is, in fact, an enclosed air-conditioned space that seats up to 100 people.

facts.fact: It received the AIA's 2006 Twenty-five Year Award and was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2000.
facts.quote: The chapel was selected by the American Institute of Architects for the 2006 Twenty-five Year Award, recognizing works whose value has continued. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places (NRHP) in 2000.

facts.fact: AIA members ranked it the fourth most favoured building in a poll.
facts.quote: In a poll of the membership of the American Institute of Architects, Thorncrown Chapel was ranked as the fourth most favored building.

facts.fact: The Röntgen Building (2007) at Bocconi, by Grafton Architects, won World Building of the Year at the 2008 World Architecture Festival.
facts.quote: Röntgen Building (2007), designed by Grafton Architects, won World Building of the Year at the 2008 World Architecture Festival in Barcelona.

facts.fact: Its designers, Yvonne Farrell and Shelley McNamara, received the 2020 Pritzker Prize.
facts.quote: Its designers, Yvonne Farrell and Shelley McNamara, received the 2020 Pritzker Architecture Prize.

facts.fact: Grafton's Bocconi building has been widely acclaimed and exhibited.
facts.quote: Their Bocconi University project in Milan, which won the World Building of the Year Award in 2008, has been widely acclaimed and exhibited.

facts.fact: The Biosphere is an environment museum in Montreal, housed in the former United States pavilion for Expo 67 on Saint Helen's Island.
facts.quote: The Biosphere, also known as the Montreal Biosphere (French: Biosphère de Montréal, pronounced [bjɔsfɛʁ də mɔ̃ʁeal]), is a museum dedicated to the environment in Montreal, Quebec, Canada. It is housed in the former United States pavilion constructed for Expo 67 located within the grounds of Parc Jean-Drapeau on Saint Helen's Island.

facts.fact: Buckminster Fuller designed the dome with Shoji Sadao and Geometrics Inc.; Cambridge Seven Associates did the interior.
facts.quote: The geodesic dome exterior was designed by R. Buckminster Fuller with Shoji Sadao and Geometrics Inc., while the interior structures and exhibits were designed by Cambridge Seven Associates.

facts.fact: Fuller first proposed a much larger dome with a suspended sphere inside for his "World Game".
facts.quote: Fuller's original proposal had entailed a much larger dome, with a suspended geodesic sphere inside it that would serve as the setting for his "World Game" project.

facts.fact: It was an enclosed dome of steel and acrylic cells, 76 m across and 62 m high, with two layers joined by a lattice of struts.
facts.quote: The building originally formed an enclosed structure of steel and acrylic cells, 76 metres (249 ft) in diameter and 62 metres (203 ft) high. It is a double-layer dome in which the inner and outer layers are connected by a latticework of struts.

facts.fact: A complex shading system controlled the temperature inside, modelled on how the body regulates its own.
facts.quote: A complex system of shades was used to control its internal temperature. The sun-shading system was an attempt by the architect to reflect the same biological processes that the human body relies on to maintain its internal temperature.

facts.fact: Visitors rode a 41 m escalator, reported as the world's longest unsupported escalator.
facts.quote: Upon entering the pavilion, visitors ascended a 41-metre (135 ft) escalator, reported to be the longest unsupported escalator in the world, to reach the exhibit platforms.

facts.fact: A fire on 20 May 1976 burned away the acrylic skin, leaving the steel frame.
facts.quote: On 20 May 1976, Biosphere was severely damaged in a fire. Sparked by a welding crew during structural renovations, the fire burned away the building's transparent acrylic bubble, but the hard steel truss structure remained.

facts.fact: The museum opened in 1995 in buildings by Éric Gauthier inside the steel skeleton.
facts.quote: The museum opened on 6 June 1995. It inhabits a set of enclosed buildings designed by Éric Gauthier, inside the original steel skeleton.

facts.fact: The Interlace is a 1,040-unit apartment complex in Singapore that looks like irregularly stacked Jenga blocks.
facts.quote: The Interlace is a 1,040-unit apartment building complex located at the boundary between Bukit Merah and Queenstown, Singapore. Noteworthy for its break from the typical tower design in cities with high population densities, it resembles Jenga blocks irregularly stacked upon each other.

facts.fact: It won World Building of the Year at the 2015 World Architecture Festival.
facts.quote: Designed by The Office for Metropolitan Architecture (OMA), it was awarded the World Building of the Year title at the 2015 World Architecture Festival.

facts.fact: It was designed by Ole Scheeren with OMA, with RSP Architects as project architects.
facts.quote: The Interlace was designed by Ole Scheeren and the architecture firm OMA. The project architects who followed the project through to completion while resolving design and compliance issues were RSP Architects Planners & Engineers.

facts.fact: It was commissioned in 2007 and finished in 2013.
facts.quote: The project was commissioned in 2007 and finished in 2013.

facts.fact: On an 8 ha site, its 31 linked blocks maximise daylight and create communal spaces.
facts.quote: The 170,000 m (560,000 ft) Interlace complex sits on 8 ha (20 acres) of land, at the corner of Depot Road and Alexandra Road. It has 31 interconnected residential blocks to maximize natural light and create communal spaces with units ranging in size from 74 m2 (800 ft2) to 590 m2 (6,300 ft2) for the penthouses at the top of each block.

facts.fact: Six-storey blocks are staggered in a hexagonal pattern around eight courtyards.
facts.quote: Interlace consists of six storey blocks staggered in a hexagonal arrangements surrounding eight courtyards.

facts.fact: Stacked four high at the centre, up to 24 floors, the blocks give almost every home a wide view.
facts.quote: The blocks are stacked four high at the center to provide maximum of 24 floors. This provides almost every home with a wide view of the surrounding areas.

facts.fact: It won the Urban Habitat Award in 2014.
facts.quote: Interlace won the Urban Habitat Award in 2014.

facts.fact: Robson Square is a civic centre and plaza in downtown Vancouver, home to the Provincial Law Courts and linked to the Vancouver Art Gallery.
facts.quote: Robson Square is a landmark civic centre and public plaza, located in Downtown Vancouver, British Columbia. It is the site of the Provincial Law Courts, UBC Robson Square, government office buildings, and public space connecting the newer development to the Vancouver Art Gallery.

facts.fact: Arthur Erickson reconceived a planned skyscraper as one laid on its back.
facts.quote: The reconceptualization Erickson came up with was of a skyscraper laid on its back, the "B.C. Centre on its back."

facts.fact: Completed 1979–1983, it covers three city blocks.
facts.quote: The new development was completed between 1979 and 1983, encompassing three city blocks and providing 1,300,000 square feet (120,774 m2) of space.

facts.fact: The glass-roofed Law Courts hold 35 courtrooms; the 420 × 115 ft glass roof sits on a steel space frame.
facts.quote: The main component is the glass-covered Law Courts, which houses 35 courtrooms in the southern block.  It is 42 metres (138 ft) in height, and the glass roof has a  size of  420 by 115 feet (128 by 35 m),  is supported by a steel space frame structure, covering approximately 50,000 square feet (4,645 m2) of public space.

facts.fact: Three cascading waterfalls provide natural air conditioning.
facts.quote: Above, three cascading waterfalls throughout the complex provide natural air conditioning with 850,000 US gallons (3,218 m3; 707,773 imp gal)  of water.

facts.fact: Like much of Erickson's work, it is mainly concrete, softened by its environmental design.
facts.quote: Typical of Erickson's designs, Robson Square is constructed primarily out of concrete, but softened by its environmental design.

facts.fact: With Cornelia Oberlander and Bing Thom, Erickson made an early green roof: the offices lie under a roof-garden plaza with waterfalls past the windows.
facts.quote: Erickson worked with Cornelia Oberlander, and his former student Bing Thom, to create one of the earliest examples of green-roof technology—as the Law Courts administrative offices are all below the plaza, it is actually a roof garden, with waterfalls cascading past office windows and skylights to drown out street noise.

facts.fact: In 2011 the RAIC gave it the Prix du XXe siècle as "a bold, contemplative work of urban design."
facts.quote: In 2011, the Royal Architectural Institute of Canada  (RAIC) awarded its Prix du XXe siècle Award to the complex, describing the concept of a "linear urban park, importing nature into the city", as "a bold, contemplative work of urban design."

facts.fact: Museo Rufino Tamayo is a public contemporary art museum in Chapultepec Park, Mexico City, built around the collection of its founder, the artist Rufino Tamayo.
facts.quote: Museo Rufino Tamayo is a public contemporary art museum located in Mexico City's Chapultepec Park, that produces contemporary art exhibitions, using its collection of modern and contemporary art, as well as artworks from the collection of its founder, the artist Rufino Tamayo.

facts.fact: The building was designed by the Mexican architects Teodoro González de León and Abraham Zabludovsky.
facts.quote: The museum building was designed by Mexican architects Teodoro González de León and Abraham Zabludovsky.

facts.fact: Both architects received Mexico's National Award of Science and Art in Fine Arts in 1982 for the design.
facts.quote: Both received the National Award of Science and Art, in the "Fine Arts" in 1982 for their design.

facts.fact: González de León and Zabludovsky designed several public buildings together between 1974 and 1982, the Museo Rufino Tamayo among them.
facts.quote: Together with him, he designed several public buildings between 1974 and 1982, amongst them the Delegación Cuauhtémoc, the COLMEX building, the seat of the Instituto del Fondo Nacional de la Vivienda para los Trabajadores (INFONAVIT), the Universidad Pedagógica Nacional and the Museo Rufino Tamayo.

facts.fact: González de León's work was influenced by Zabludovsky after 1969.
facts.quote: After 1969, his work was influenced by Abraham Zabludovsky.

facts.fact: The museum's modern collection includes artists such as Picasso, Miró, Francis Bacon, Rothko and Warhol.
facts.quote: The modern collection is striking for the list of major artists represented in it: Pablo Picasso, Joan Miró, Francis Bacon, Jean Dubuffet, Fernand Léger, Wifredo Lam, Pierre Soulages, Frank Auerbach, Alexander Calder, Eduardo Chillida, Salvador Dalí, Max Ernst, Josep Guinovart, Barbara Hepworth, Hans Hartung, Willem de Kooning, Roy Lichtenstein, René Magritte, Manolo Millares, Robert Motherwell, Georgia O´Keeffe, Arnaldo Pomodoro, Mark Rothko, Antoni Tàpies, Joaquín Torres García, Victor Vasarely, Andy Warhol, among others.

facts.fact: The Niterói Contemporary Art Museum (MAC) is in the city of Niterói, Rio de Janeiro state, Brazil, and is one of the city's main landmarks.
facts.quote: The Niterói Contemporary Art Museum (Museu de Arte Contemporânea de Niterói — MAC) is situated in the city of Niterói, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, and is one of the city’s main landmarks.

facts.fact: It was completed in 1996.
facts.quote: It was completed in 1996.

facts.fact: Oscar Niemeyer designed it with the structural engineer Bruno Contarini, who had worked with him on earlier projects.
facts.quote: The MAC-Niterói was designed by Oscar Niemeyer with the assistance of structural engineer Bruno Contarini, who had worked with Niemeyer on earlier projects.

facts.fact: The structure is 16 metres high, and its cupola is 50 metres across with three floors.
facts.quote: The structure is 16 meters high; its cupola has a diameter of 50 meters with three floors.

facts.fact: It projects over Boa Viagem beach, and an 817 m² reflecting pool surrounds its cylindrical base "like a flower", in Niemeyer's words.
facts.quote: The museum projects itself over Boa Viagem (“Bon Voyage,” “Good Journey”) beach and also a neighborhood, the 817 square metres (8,790 sq ft) reflecting pool that surrounds the cylindrical base “like a flower,” in the words of Niemeyer.

facts.fact: A wide access ramp leads to the exhibition hall.
facts.quote: A wide access slope leads to a Hall of Expositions, which has a capacity for sixty people.

facts.fact: Two doors lead to a viewing gallery that looks out over Guanabara Bay, Rio de Janeiro and Sugarloaf Mountain.
facts.quote: Two doors lead to the viewing gallery, through which can be seen Guanabara Bay, Rio de Janeiro, and Sugarloaf Mountain.

facts.fact: The saucer-shaped modernist building, often likened to a UFO, sits on a cliff above a beach.
facts.quote: The saucer-shaped modernist structure, which has been likened to a UFO, is set on a cliffside, at the bottom of which is a beach.

facts.fact: The museum holds 1,217 works from the collection of João Sattamini.
facts.quote: The museum has a collection of 1,217 works from the art collector João Sattamini.

facts.fact: The Gustavo Capanema Palace, also known as the Ministry of Education and Health Building, is a government office building in downtown Rio de Janeiro.
facts.quote: The Gustavo Capanema Palace (Portuguese: Palácio Gustavo Capanema), also known architecturally as the Ministry of Education and Health Building, is a government office building in downtown Rio de Janeiro, Brazil.

facts.fact: As Brazil's first modernist project it is key to the history of Modernism in the country, and it is on Brazil's UNESCO tentative list.
facts.quote: As the first modernist project in Brazil, it is historically important to the architectural development of Modernism in the country and has been placed on Brazil's UNESCO tentative list.

facts.fact: It was designed by a team led by Lucio Costa with Affonso Eduardo Reidy, Ernani Vasconcellos, Carlos Leão, Jorge Machado Moreira and Roberto Burle Marx.
facts.quote: It was designed by a team composed of Lucio Costa (future designer of the master plan of Brazil's modernist capital Brasília), along with Affonso Eduardo Reidy, Ernani Vasconcellos, Carlos Leão, Jorge Machado Moreira, and Roberto Burle Marx.

facts.fact: Oscar Niemeyer worked on it as an intern in Costa's office, and the team invited Le Corbusier to oversee the project.
facts.quote: Oscar Niemeyer, who became Brazil's best-known architect later, had a role as an intern in Costa's office. The group invited renowned Swiss-French Modernist architect Le Corbusier to oversee the project.

facts.fact: Construction ran from 1939 to 1945, to house Brazil's new Ministry of Education and Health.
facts.quote: Construction was begun by the Getúlio Vargas government in 1939 and was completed in 1945, to house Brazil's new Ministry of Education and Health.

facts.fact: Although it is a 15-storey office block, it is raised on pilotis, leaving the ground open to the surrounding pavements.
facts.quote: Despite being a large office building of 15 stories, the structure has a distinct lightness to it, as it is raised 3 floors above the sidewalk on pilotis (pillars) with access unobstructed from surrounding sidewalks and pedestrian areas.

facts.fact: A concrete frame let both long sides be fully glazed, and the sunny north glass is shaded by adjustable brise-soleil, the first system of its kind in the world.
facts.quote: An internal concrete frame allowed the two broad sides of the building to be entirely of glass. Tropical sunshine on northern glass walls is controlled by Corbusian brises-soleil (sun-shades) made adjustable in a system that was the first of its kind in the world.

facts.fact: It uses local materials such as azulejos, blue and white glazed tiles from the Portuguese colonial tradition, in modern wall murals.
facts.quote: It also employed local materials and techniques, such as azulejos, blue and white glazed tiles linked to the Portuguese Colonial tradition, in modern wall murals.

facts.fact: Roberto Burle Marx laid out modernist tropical gardens using native Brazilian plants.
facts.quote: Modernist tropical gardens were laid out by the great landscape architect Roberto Burle Marx, and included native plants of Brazil the plant palette, unique at the time.

facts.fact: Pedregulho is an apartment complex and planned community in the São Cristóvão neighbourhood of Rio de Janeiro.
facts.quote: The Pedregulho Housing Complex (Portuguese: Conjunto Residencial Prefeito Mendes de Moraes, commonly known as Pedregulho) is an apartment complex and planned community in the São Cristóvão neighborhood of Rio de Janeiro, Brazil.

facts.fact: It was designed by Affonso Eduardo Reidy, with his partner Carmen Portinho as chief engineer.
facts.quote: It was designed by the architect Affonso Eduardo Reidy (1909-1964) with his partner Carmen Portinho serving as the chief engineer.

facts.fact: It was planned in 1946 to house lower-paid civil servants of the city.
facts.quote: The project was planned in 1946 to house lower-paid civil servants of the city, which was then the Federal District of Brazil.

facts.fact: The main building is a long serpentine block raised on pilotis.
facts.quote: The main apartment building consists of a long, serpentine block suspended above pilotis.

facts.fact: It holds 272 flats on seven storeys, and Reidy tried to give every flat a view of Guanabara Bay.
facts.quote: 272 units are placed on seven stories. Reidy attempted to provide a view of Guanabara Bay from each apartment unit.

facts.fact: The only entrance is by two bridges to the third floor at the middle of the block, which avoided the need for lifts.
facts.quote: The single entrance to the building is via two gangplanks that lead to the third floor; its location at the middle of the building mitigated the need for elevators.

facts.fact: The third floor holds offices, a children's theatre, a nursery and a kindergarten.
facts.quote: The third floor is reserved for administrative offices, a children's theater, nursery, and kindergarten.

facts.fact: The complex originally included a services building, shops, a nursery, a primary school, sports courts, a gymnasium, a pool and a health centre.
facts.quote: The complex, in its original form, included a public services building, shopping center, children's garden, nursery, primary school, sports courts, gymnasium, swimming pool, and health center.

facts.fact: It won first prize at the International Architecture Competition of the 1st São Paulo Biennial in 1951.
facts.quote: It won first prize at the International Architecture Competition at the 1st Biennial of São Paulo in 1951.

facts.fact: Restoration of the serpentine building began in 2010 and was completed in 2015.
facts.quote: Restoration of the iconic serpentine building began in 2010 and was completed in 2015.

facts.fact: The Pinacoteca de São Paulo is an art museum focused on Brazilian art from the 19th century to today.
facts.quote: The Pinacoteca de São Paulo (Portuguese for "pinacotheca (picture gallery) of the state of São Paulo") is a visual arts museum focused on Brazilian art from the 19th century to the present day, in dialogue with various cultures from around the world.

facts.fact: Founded in 1905, it is the oldest art museum in the city.
facts.quote: Founded in 1905 by the Government of the State of São Paulo, the Pinacoteca is the oldest art museum in the city and has three buildings: Pinacoteca Luz, Pinacoteca Estação and Pinacoteca Contemporânea.

facts.fact: Its main building, designed by Ramos de Azevedo and Domiciano Rossi in Italian eclectic style, has three floors around two internal courtyards for air and light.
facts.quote: The building, designed by Ramos de Azevedo and Domiciano Rossi, his main collaborator, has a monumental style in strong harmony with the principles of Italian eclecticism, consisting of three floors, with two internal courtyards to ensure ventilation and lighting.

facts.fact: The building was never completed: its bricks were left exposed and the planned dome was never built.
facts.quote: However, the building was never completed, as evidenced by the exposed bricks on the façade and in the internal courtyards and the absence of the aforementioned dome, which was part of the original project.

facts.fact: Between 1993 and 1998 Paulo Mendes da Rocha, with Weliton Ricoy Torres and Eduardo Argenton Colonelli, renovated it into a museum fit for international exhibitions.
facts.quote: Between 1993 and 1998, the main building underwent extensive renovations led by architect Paulo Mendes da Rocha, together with architects Weliton Ricoy Torres and Eduardo Argenton Colonelli, which resulted in a museum adapted to the needs of international exhibitions, making the Pinacoteca do Estado a popular destination for many of the exhibitions that come to São Paulo.

facts.fact: The renovation won the three architects the Mies van der Rohe Prize for Latin America.
facts.quote: The renovation project was awarded the Mies van der Rohe Prize for Latin America to the three architects.

facts.fact: The building was listed in 1982 as part of the historic ensemble of the Luz neighbourhood.
facts.quote: The building was officially listed in 1982, with the aim of preserving one of the components of the architectural ensemble of the Luz neighborhood, characteristic of the turn of the 19th to the 20th century in São Paulo, which also includes the Luz Station, Júlio Prestes Station, the São Paulo Museum of Sacred Art, among others.

facts.fact: The Mariano Moreno National Library is the largest library in Argentina.
facts.quote: The Mariano Moreno National Library (Spanish: Biblioteca Nacional Mariano Moreno) is the largest library in Argentina.

facts.fact: It is in the Recoleta district of Buenos Aires.
facts.quote: It is located in the barrio of Recoleta in Buenos Aires.

facts.fact: After the Unzué Palace was demolished in 1958, its grounds were set aside for the library's new main building.
facts.quote: Following a politically motivated demolition of the Unzué Palace in 1958, the grounds were designated for the library's new main building.

facts.fact: The brutalist building was designed in 1961, but construction did not start until 1971.
facts.quote: The brutalist structure was designed in 1961, though construction did not begin until 1971.

facts.fact: The new library opened on 10 April 1992.
facts.quote: The new library was inaugurated on April 10, 1992.

facts.fact: Changes of government and indifference to culture delayed the project, designed by Clorindo Testa, Francisco Bullrich and Alicia Cazzaniga.
facts.quote: The successive changes in government leadership and bureaucracies, along with certain indifferences towards cultural matters were factors that delayed the project originally envisioned by the architectural team of Clorindo Testa, Francisco Bullrich, and Alicia Cazzaniga.

facts.fact: Eero Saarinen designed the main terminal in 1958, and it is admired for a graceful form that suggests flight.
facts.quote: The main terminal was designed in 1958 by famed Finnish-American architect Eero Saarinen, and it is highly regarded for its graceful beauty, suggestive of flight.

facts.fact: The terminal was built without concourses or gates, because all aircraft parked at remote stands.
facts.quote: The terminal was built without any concourses and gates as all aircraft were parked at remote sites.

facts.fact: Passengers reached their planes in mobile lounges that rose to aircraft level, and some are still in use.
facts.quote: Passengers were bussed to their aircraft by way of mobile lounges that raised up to the aircraft level; some are still in use today.

facts.fact: The American Institute of Architects recognised the terminal in 1966; its roof is a suspended catenary that encloses a wide space with no columns.
facts.quote: The main terminal was recognized by the American Institute of Architects in 1966 for its design concept; its roof is a suspended catenary providing a wide enclosed area unimpeded by any columns.

facts.fact: In 1996 the terminal was extended to 1,240 feet, Saarinen's original design length, more than double the 600 feet first built.
facts.quote: The main terminal was extended in 1996 to 1,240 feet (380 m)—Saarinen's original design length—which was slightly more than double its originally constructed length of 600 feet (180 m).

facts.fact: The original terminal at Taiwan Taoyuan International Airport was modelled on Saarinen's terminal at Dulles.
facts.quote: The original terminal at Taiwan Taoyuan International Airport in Taoyuan, Taiwan, was modeled after the Saarinen terminal at Dulles.

facts.fact: Many of Saarinen's projects, including this one, use catenary curves in their structure.
facts.quote: Many of these projects use catenary curves in their structural designs.

facts.fact: The TWA Flight Center is a building at John F. Kennedy International Airport in Queens, New York.
facts.quote: The TWA Flight Center (also known as the Trans World Flight Center or TWA Terminal) is a building at John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) in Queens, New York, United States.

facts.fact: Eero Saarinen and Associates designed it for Trans World Airlines; it was completed in 1962 and served as a terminal for four decades.
facts.quote: Designed by Eero Saarinen and Associates for Trans World Airlines (TWA), the building was completed in 1962 and operated as an airport terminal for four decades.

facts.fact: Its thin concrete shell roof is shaped like a bird's wings and stands on four Y-shaped piers.
facts.quote: The headhouse has a thin shell concrete roof, shaped like a set of bird's wings and supported by four Y-shaped piers.

facts.fact: Inside is an open three-level space with large windows that once looked over the airfield.
facts.quote: Inside is an open, three-level space with large windows; the windows overlooked the tarmac before Terminal 5 and the TWA Hotel's towers were built.

facts.fact: Two tube-shaped, red-carpeted corridors lead out from the main hall.
facts.quote: The TWA Flight Center also includes two tube-shaped, red-carpeted departure and arrival corridors extending outward from the headhouse.

facts.fact: It was among the first terminals to use enclosed passenger jetways.
facts.quote: The TWA Flight Center was among the first to use enclosed passenger jetways, which connected with flight wings (structures with airline gates).

facts.fact: The main hall became part of the TWA Hotel in 2019.
facts.quote: The building's main section, the headhouse, was repurposed as part of the TWA Hotel in 2019.

facts.fact: The interior and exterior are New York City landmarks, and the building is on the National Register of Historic Places.
facts.quote: The original design was widely acclaimed; the interior and the exterior of the headhouse are New York City designated landmarks, and the building is on the National Register of Historic Places.

facts.fact: The Gateway Arch is a 630-foot (192 m) monument in St. Louis, Missouri.
facts.quote: The Gateway Arch is a 630-foot-tall (192 m) monument in St. Louis, Missouri, United States.

facts.fact: Clad in stainless steel and shaped as a weighted catenary, it is the world's tallest arch.
facts.quote: Clad in stainless steel and built in the form of a weighted catenary arch, it is the world's tallest arch and Missouri's tallest accessible structure.

facts.fact: Eero Saarinen designed it in 1947.
facts.quote: The Arch was designed by the Finnish-American architect Eero Saarinen in 1947.

facts.fact: Construction ran from February 1963 to October 1965.
facts.quote: Construction began on February 12, 1963, and was completed on October 28, 1965, at an overall cost of $13 million (equivalent to $101 million in 2025).

facts.fact: On 18 February 1948 the jury unanimously chose Saarinen's design in the competition.
facts.quote: The deadline for the second stage arrived on February 10, 1948, and on February 18, the jury chose Saarinen's design unanimously, praising its "profoundly evocative and truly monumental expression." The following day, during a formal dinner at Statler Hotel that the finalists and the media attended, Wurster pronounced Saarinen the winner of the competition and awarded the checks—$40,000 to his team and $50,000 to Saarinen.

facts.fact: The sculptor Carl Milles advised Saarinen to make the base of each leg a triangle rather than a square.
facts.quote: In the first stage of the competition, Carl Milles advised Saarinen to change the bases of each leg to triangles instead of squares.

facts.fact: It was built from 142 prefabricated stainless steel sections, each with a double-walled skin filled with concrete.
facts.quote: The arch was assembled of 142 12-foot-long (3.7 m) prefabricated stainless steel sections. Once in place, each section had its double-walled skin filled with concrete, prestressed with 252 tension bars.

facts.fact: Built to mark the westward expansion of the United States, it is a National Historic Landmark and a symbol of St. Louis.
facts.quote: Built as a monument to the westward expansion of the United States and officially dedicated to "the American people", the Arch, commonly referred to as "The Gateway to the West", is a National Historic Landmark in Gateway Arch National Park and has become a popular tourist destination, as well as an internationally recognized symbol of St. Louis.

facts.fact: The Frederick C. Robie House is a house museum on the University of Chicago campus in Chicago's Hyde Park.
facts.quote: The Frederick C. Robie House is a historic house museum on the University of Chicago campus in the Hyde Park neighborhood of Chicago, Illinois, United States.

facts.fact: Frank Lloyd Wright designed it in the Prairie style, and it was completed in 1910.
facts.quote: Designed by the architect Frank Lloyd Wright in the Prairie style, it was completed in 1910.

facts.fact: Its open plan is made of two large offset rectangles, called "vessels".
facts.quote: The house's open floor plan consists of two large, offset rectangles known as "vessels".

facts.fact: The walls are mostly Roman brick, with concrete trim, cut stone and art glass windows.
facts.quote: The facade and perimeter walls are made largely of Roman brick, with concrete trim, cut-stone decorations, and art glass windows.

facts.fact: Terraces sit at different levels, and the roofs are cantilevered outward.
facts.quote: The massing includes several terraces, which are placed on different levels, in addition to roofs that are cantilevered outward.

facts.fact: Its roofs cantilever out from the house's core instead of resting on load-bearing walls.
facts.quote: Unlike similar houses, whose roofs are supported from underneath by load-bearing walls, the Robie House's roofs are cantilevered outward from the house's core.

facts.fact: The house was highly influential, helping to popularise picture windows, projecting roofs and attached garages.
facts.quote: The Robie House was highly influential, having helped popularize design details such as picture windows, protruding roofs, and attached garages in residential architecture.

facts.fact: It is a National Historic Landmark and part of the World Heritage Site "The 20th-Century Architecture of Frank Lloyd Wright".
facts.quote: The Robie House is designated as a Chicago Landmark and a National Historic Landmark, and it forms part of The 20th-Century Architecture of Frank Lloyd Wright, a designated World Heritage Site.

facts.fact: Unity Temple is a Unitarian Universalist church in Oak Park, Illinois.
facts.quote: Unity Temple is a Unitarian Universalist church building that houses the Unity Temple Unitarian Universalist Congregation at 875 Lake Street in Oak Park, Illinois, United States.

facts.fact: Frank Lloyd Wright designed it in the Prairie style, and it is cited as an early example of modern architecture.
facts.quote: The structure, designed by the architect Frank Lloyd Wright in the Prairie style, is cited as an early example of modern architecture.

facts.fact: It has an auditorium to the north and a church house, Unity House, to the south, joined by an entrance pavilion, all of reinforced concrete.
facts.quote: The building consists of an auditorium to the north and a church house called Unity House to the south. The two sections, and an entrance pavilion between them, are made of reinforced concrete.

facts.fact: The facade is Portland cement washed back to expose the gravel, with recessed clerestory windows near the top.
facts.quote: The facade is made of Portland cement, which has been washed away to expose the gravel underneath; there are recessed clerestory windows near the top.

facts.fact: It has no spire; the roof is a set of flat, overhanging concrete slabs.
facts.quote: Unlike contemporary churches, Unity Temple was designed without a spire; instead, the roof consists of multiple flat, overhanging concrete slabs.

facts.fact: The auditorium is a Greek cross with stair towers at each corner, two levels of seating around a central pulpit, and clerestories and skylights.
facts.quote: The auditorium is shaped like a Greek cross, with stair towers at each corner. It has two levels of seating surrounding a central pulpit, in addition to clerestories and skylights.

facts.fact: It is decorated with abstract motifs rather than religious imagery.
facts.quote: The temple is decorated with abstract motifs instead of overtly religious imagery.

facts.fact: It is a National Historic Landmark and part of the World Heritage Site "The 20th-Century Architecture of Frank Lloyd Wright".
facts.quote: Unity Temple is designated as a National Historic Landmark and is part of The 20th-Century Architecture of Frank Lloyd Wright, a World Heritage Site.

facts.fact: The Toronto-Dominion Centre is a complex of office towers in the Financial District of downtown Toronto.
facts.quote: The Toronto-Dominion Centre, or TD Centre, is a skyscraper complex in the Financial District of downtown Toronto, Ontario, Canada.

facts.fact: It is made of six towers and a pavilion clad in bronze-tinted glass and black-painted steel.
facts.quote: The complex consists of six towers and a pavilion covered in bronze-tinted glass and black-painted steel.

facts.fact: Mies van der Rohe was officially the design consultant to the local architects, but the project was essentially his design.
facts.quote: Though he was technically commissioned as the design consultant to the local architects (who were still John B. Parkin and Associates, but partnered with Bregman + Hamann Architects), the project was essentially Mies's design in its entirety, demonstrating all the key characteristics of the architect's unique style.

facts.fact: It was Mies's last major work before his death in 1969.
facts.quote: It also marked Mies's last major work before his death in 1969.

facts.fact: The buildings stand on a granite plinth, all ordered by a 1.5 m grid.
facts.quote: The TD Centre, however, comprises a collection of structures spread across a granite plinth, all regulated in three dimensions and from the largest scale to the smallest, by a mathematically ordered, 1.5 m2 (16 sq ft) grid.

facts.fact: The granite paving follows the grid and runs through the glass lobbies, blurring inside and outside.
facts.quote: The rectilinear pattern of Saint-Jean granite pavers follows the grid, serving to organize and unify the complex, and the plaza's surface material extends through the glass lobbies of the towers and the banking pavilion, blurring the distinction between interior and exterior space.

facts.fact: The banking pavilion's roof is a waffle grid of deep steel I-beams resting on evenly spaced columns around its edge.
facts.quote: The roof of the building is made of deep steel I-sections, each beam supported on only one steel I-section column at each end, all combined to create a waffle-grid ceiling resting on a row of corresponding, equally spaced columns around the periphery.

facts.fact: It has been a protected heritage property under the Ontario Heritage Act since 2003.
facts.quote: The complex has been designated under Part IV of the Ontario Heritage Act since 2003.

facts.fact: The John Hancock Center, now 875 North Michigan Avenue, is a 100-storey, 344-metre skyscraper in Chicago.
facts.quote: 875 North Michigan Avenue (formerly known as and still commonly referred to as the John Hancock Center) is a 100-story, 1,128-foot-tall (344-meter) skyscraper located in Chicago, Illinois.

facts.fact: It was designed by the chief designer Bruce Graham and the structural engineer Fazlur Rahman Khan of Skidmore, Owings and Merrill (SOM).
facts.quote: Located in the Magnificent Mile district, the building was designed by Peruvian-American chief designer Bruce Graham and Bangladeshi-American structural engineer Fazlur Rahman Khan of Skidmore, Owings and Merrill (SOM).

facts.fact: When it topped out in 1968 it was the world's second-tallest building after the Empire State Building.
facts.quote: When the building topped out on May 6, 1968, it was the second-tallest building in the world after the Empire State Building, in New York City, and the tallest in Chicago.

facts.fact: It holds offices, restaurants and about 700 flats, and on completion it had the highest residence in the world.
facts.quote: The building is home to several offices and restaurants, as well as about 700 condominiums; at the time of its completion, it contained the highest residence in the world.

facts.fact: Its X-braced exterior shows that the skin is part of the structure's "tubular system".
facts.quote: One of the most famous buildings of the structural expressionist style, the skyscraper's distinctive X-braced exterior shows that the structure's skin is part of its "tubular system".

facts.fact: The X-bracing lets tall buildings perform better and opens up the floor plan inside.
facts.quote: This X-bracing allows for both higher performance from tall structures and the ability to open up the inside floorplan.

facts.fact: It was the first tower to have a "sky lobby", where residents change from express lifts to local ones.
facts.quote: The tower was the first in the world to introduce a 'sky lobby' where express elevators from the ground floor stop, and residents then transfer to 'local' elevators to get to their own floor.

facts.fact: It won the American Institute of Architects' Twenty-five Year Award in 1999.
facts.quote: It has won various awards for its distinctive style, including the Distinguished Architects Twenty-five Year Award from the American Institute of Architects in May 1999.

facts.fact: The PSFS Building, now the Loews Philadelphia Hotel, is a skyscraper in Center City, Philadelphia.
facts.quote: The PSFS Building, also known as the Loews Philadelphia Hotel, is a skyscraper in Center City, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania.

facts.fact: It was the first International Style skyscraper built in the United States, designed by William Lescaze and George Howe for the Philadelphia Saving Fund Society.
facts.quote: The building, the first International Style skyscraper constructed in the United States, was designed by architects William Lescaze and George Howe, was built for the Philadelphia Saving (later Savings) Fund Society.

facts.fact: The design broke with traditional bank architecture, leaving out domes and ornament.
facts.quote: The skyscraper's design was a departure from traditional bank and Philadelphia architecture, lacking features such as domes and ornamentation.

facts.fact: Its T-shaped tower lets maximum light into the office floors and stresses the banking hall at the base.
facts.quote: The t-shaped tower was designed in a way to allow in the maximum amount of light on the office floors and to emphasize the banking portion in the base.

facts.fact: It was the first skyscraper to show its spine of lifts and services on the outside rather than hiding it in the centre.
facts.quote: The building's spine containing elevators and utilities was made visible on the outside for the first time in a skyscraper instead of hidden inside in the center of the building.

facts.fact: It was the second high-rise in the US to have air conditioning.
facts.quote: The building was the second high-rise in the U.S. to be equipped with air conditioning.

facts.fact: A red neon PSFS sign on top, visible for 20 miles, has become a Philadelphia icon.
facts.quote: The skyscraper is topped by a red neon sign with the PSFS initials. Visible for 20 miles (32 km), the sign has become a Philadelphia icon.

facts.fact: It was listed as a National Historic Landmark in 1976 for its architecture.
facts.quote: The PSFS Building was listed as a National Historic Landmark in 1976 because of its architectural significance.

facts.fact: The Ford Foundation Building, now the Ford Foundation Center for Social Justice, is a 12-storey office building in East Midtown Manhattan.
facts.quote: The Ford Foundation Center for Social Justice (also known as 320 East 43rd Street, 321 East 42nd Street, or the Ford Foundation Building) is a 12-story office building in East Midtown Manhattan, New York City, United States.

facts.fact: Completed in 1967, it was designed in the late modernist style by Kevin Roche and John Dinkeloo.
facts.quote: Completed in 1967, it was designed in the late modernist style by architect Kevin Roche and engineering partner John Dinkeloo of Roche-Dinkeloo.

facts.fact: It is a glass-and-steel cube on concrete piers clad in Dakota granite.
facts.quote: The building is a glass-and-steel cube held up by piers made of concrete, clad with Dakota granite.

facts.fact: Dan Kiley landscaped its large public atrium, the first in a Manhattan office building, with trees, shrubs and vines.
facts.quote: Dan Kiley was the landscape architect for the large public atrium inside, the first such space in an office building in Manhattan; it includes trees, shrubs, vines, and other plants.

facts.fact: The atrium is about 30 by 30 metres in plan and 49 metres high.
facts.quote: The Ford Foundation Building is built around a 1⁄3-acre (0.13 ha) public atrium with a 100-by-100-foot (30 by 30 m) square floor plan and a 160-foot-high (49 m) ceiling.

facts.fact: The facade uses Cor-Ten steel, left to weather to a deep tan.
facts.quote: The facade also uses Cor-Ten steel, particularly in sections of the building that overhang other spaces. The steel was allowed to weather to a deep tan color.

facts.fact: The offices sit in narrow wings on the north and west sides of the atrium, like a Spanish courtyard building.
facts.quote: Above ground level, most of the upper stories are composed of narrow wings on the northern and western sides of the atrium, arranged similarly to Spanish buildings with interior courtyards.

facts.fact: It was restored in 2015–2018; the building and its atrium are New York City landmarks.
facts.quote: The building underwent a major renovation and restoration between 2015 and 2018, and it was renamed the "Ford Foundation Center for Social Justice". The structure received critical acclaim for its design following both completion and renovation, and the New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission has designated the building and its atrium as city landmarks.

facts.fact: The Wainwright Building is a 10-storey terracotta office building in downtown St. Louis, Missouri.
facts.quote: The Wainwright Building (formerly the Missouri Insurance Building and Wainwright State Office Building) is a 10-story, 135-foot (41 m) terra cotta office building at 709 Chestnut Street in Downtown St. Louis, Missouri.

facts.fact: It is considered one of the first early skyscrapers to be fully expressed aesthetically.
facts.quote: The Wainwright Building is considered to be one of the first aesthetically fully expressed early skyscrapers.

facts.fact: Dankmar Adler and Louis Sullivan designed it, and it was built in 1890–1891.
facts.quote: It was designed by Dankmar Adler and Louis Sullivan and built between 1890 and 1891.

facts.fact: It follows Sullivan's three-part composition of base, shaft and attic, based on the classical column, and stresses its height.
facts.quote: Aesthetically, the Wainwright Building exemplifies Sullivan's theories about the tall building, which included a tripartite (three-part) composition (base-shaft-attic) based on the structure of the classical column, and his desire to emphasize the height of the building.

facts.fact: A wide frieze of Sullivan's leaf ornament runs below the deep cornice, with decorated spandrels between the windows.
facts.quote: The ornamentation for the building includes a wide frieze below the deep cornice, which expresses the formalized yet naturalistic celery-leaf foliage typical of Sullivan and published in his System of Architectural Ornament, decorated spandrels between the windows on the different floors and an elaborate door surround at the main entrance.

facts.fact: Frank Lloyd Wright called it "the very first human expression of a tall steel office-building as Architecture."
facts.quote: Architect Frank Lloyd Wright called the Wainwright Building "the very first human expression of a tall steel office-building as Architecture."

facts.fact: It became a National Historic Landmark in 1968 and a city landmark in 1972.
facts.quote: In 1968, the building was designated as a National Historic Landmark and in 1972 it was named a city landmark.

facts.fact: In 2000 the Toledo Museum of Art chose SANAA to design a new building for its glass collection.
facts.quote: In 2000, the museum chose the architectural firm of SANAA to design a new building to house the institution's glass collection.

facts.fact: It was SANAA's first commission in the United States.
facts.quote: It was the firm's first commission in the United States.

facts.fact: Front Inc. helped the architects develop the glass wall systems.
facts.quote: Front Inc. was appointed to assist the architects in developing technical concepts for the glass wall systems.

facts.fact: Its curved glass walls were imported from China.
facts.quote: The building's curved glass walls were imported from China.

facts.fact: The 74,000-square-foot Glass Pavilion opened in August 2006 to wide critical acclaim.
facts.quote: The 74,000-square foot Glass Pavilion opened in August 2006 to considerable critical acclaim.

facts.fact: The New York Times critic Nicolai Ouroussoff described its "elegant maze of curved glass walls".
facts.quote: In his review for The New York Times, Nicolai Ouroussoff wrote, "Composed with exquisite delicacy, the pavilion's elegant maze of curved glass walls represents the latest monument to evolve in a chain extending back to the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles."

facts.fact: Its low, horizontal form sits delicately beside the museum's older buildings.
facts.quote: The new structure's low, horizontal form, fits in this context with remarkable delicacy, as if the architects hesitated to disturb the surroundings."

facts.fact: Arata Isozaki's notable works include the Museum of Modern Art, Gunma (1974) in Takasaki.
facts.quote: Museum of Modern Art, Gunma (1974) in Takasaki, Japan

facts.fact: Aiko Miyawaki's sculpture series Utsurohi is installed at the Gunma Museum of Modern Art.
facts.quote: Gunma Museum of Modern Art, Takasaki

facts.fact: The Hachioji library of Tama Art University, designed by Toyo Ito, is seen as an architectural achievement for its concept and construction.
facts.quote: Designed by architect Toyo Ito, the newer of the two libraries that make up Tama Art University Library, the Hachioji location, is viewed as an architectural achievement due to its unique concept and construction.

facts.fact: It stands between the university's main gate and the centre of campus, and opened in 2007 after three years of building.
facts.quote: The Hachioji Library, situated between Tama Art University's main gate and the center of campus, opened in 2007 after three years of construction.

facts.fact: It is built of steel and concrete, two storeys high with a basement.
facts.quote: The building was constructed using both steel and concrete, is two stories high, and also has a basement.

facts.fact: The ground floor follows a gentle three-degree slope, and colonnades of arches carry the structure.
facts.quote: The library takes advantage of a gentle, three-degree slope on its ground floor, with colonnades providing simple, archlike structural support.

facts.fact: The arches are plate steel reinforced with concrete, 200 mm thick, spanning up to more than 12 metres.
facts.quote: These arches are formed with plate steel reinforced with concrete, with walls measuring 200 millimeters (about 7.8 inches) thick, with a maximum span of more than 12 meters (39 feet).

facts.fact: The steel and concrete arches and the glass walls around them follow the land the library sits on.
facts.quote: The building's arches, made of steel and concrete, along with the surrounding glass walls, flow with the land that the library sits on.

facts.fact: Kazuko Fujie designed furniture and shelves to suit the sloping floors and the arches.
facts.quote: The furniture was specially designed in a similar way, by Fujie Kazuko, to accommodate the landscape's sloping surfaces. Kazuko also created shelves that further balance the aesthetic of the arches with the building's angled floors.

facts.fact: Visits rose from 38,000 at the old library in 2006 to 86,000 at the new one in 2012.
facts.quote: “In 2006, the old library had 38,000 visitors, while in 2012 the new library recorded 86,000 visits,” according to The Guardian interviewer Claire Shaw.

facts.fact: The Suzhou Museum holds ancient Chinese art, paintings, calligraphy and crafts in Suzhou, China.
facts.quote: The Suzhou Museum (Chinese: 蘇州博物館; pinyin: Sūzhōu Bówùguǎn) is a museum of ancient Chinese art, paintings, calligraphy and handmade crafts in Suzhou, Jiangsu, China.

facts.fact: The building was designed by I. M. Pei with Pei Partnership Architects.
facts.quote: The Suzhou Museum building was designed by Pritzker Prize-winning architect I.M. Pei in association with Pei Partnership Architects.

facts.fact: Construction began in 2002, and the building opened on 6 October 2006.
facts.quote: Construction began in 2002 and the building was inaugurated on October 6, 2006.

facts.fact: Pei blended traditional Chinese design, local Suzhou character and modern design.
facts.quote: Pei designed the museum using a blend of traditional Chinese design, local Suzhou flavor, and modern design.

facts.fact: Sloping roofs, a black, white and grey palette and white stucco walls recall the old city.
facts.quote: The essence of the old city is represented in the sloping roofs, a traditional color palette of black, white, and gray and traditional white stucco walls.

facts.fact: Glass in the roof, a steel frame instead of timber beams, and dark granite roof tiles make it modern; the stone and glass roof lets in daylight controlled by metal sunshades.
facts.quote: These include glass incorporated into the roof, a steel structure that replaces traditional wooden beam and rafter framing, and "China black" granite roof tiles instead of traditional brick tiles. The stone and glass roof admits natural light, which is regulated by metal sunshades.

facts.fact: Its main courtyard lies beside the Humble Administrator's Garden, the largest of Suzhou's classical gardens.
facts.quote: The north side of the courtyard is next to the Humble Administrator's Garden, the largest of Suzhou's classical gardens.

facts.fact: Pei built the design from simple shapes such as octagons, rhombuses and triangles.
facts.quote: Pei used simple geometric shapes such as octagons, rhombuses, and triangles as the building blocks of the museum's design.

facts.fact: The Harbin Grand Theatre, or Harbin Opera House, is a multi-venue performing arts centre in Harbin, China.
facts.quote: The Harbin Grand Theatre or Harbin Opera House (Chinese: 哈尔滨大剧院; pinyin: Hā'ěrbīn Dàjùyuàn) is a multi-venue performing arts centre in Harbin, Heilongjiang Province, China.

facts.fact: It was designed by MAD, the Chinese practice led by Ma Yansong.
facts.quote: Measuring 850,349 square feet, the theatre is designed by well-known Chinese architect agency MAD led by Ma Yansong.

facts.fact: It is the centrepiece of Harbin's Cultural Island, an arts district by the Songhua River and its wetlands.
facts.quote: The building serves as the centerpiece of Harbin's Cultural Island—an arts hub by the Songhua River and surrounding wetlands in suburban Harbin.

facts.fact: The theatre is clad entirely in white aluminium panels.
facts.quote: The theatre is clad entirely in white aluminium panels.

facts.fact: Inside are white walls, skylights and timber.
facts.quote: There is a structure inside the opera house with contemporary white walls, skylights and timber.

facts.fact: Paths are carved into the facade, and visitors can climb to the top of the building.
facts.quote: There are carved paths on the façade of the building. Visitors are able to climb up to the top of the building for sightseeing.

facts.fact: Ma wanted the snow-white building to feel calm, unlike the towering landmarks of many Chinese cities.
facts.quote: Ma wanted its snow-white structure to have a soothing aesthetic, in contrast to modern landmark buildings in Chinese cities which are often towering and imposing.

facts.fact: The architect meant it to read as an extension of the surrounding wetlands, waterways and snowy land.
facts.quote: The architect emphasized the building's integration to nature as an extension of surrounding wetlands, waterways, and snowy terrain.

facts.fact: It won ArchDaily's 2016 Building of the Year award.
facts.quote: The Harbin Grand Theatre won the ArchDaily 2016 Building of the Year Award, WAN Performing Spaces Award 2016 and 2017 IALD Award.

facts.fact: Tai Kwun, the former Central Police Station compound in Central, Hong Kong, includes three declared monuments: the police station, the magistracy and Victoria Prison.
facts.quote: Tai Kwun, or the Former Central Police Station Compound (CPS Compound) includes three declared monuments in Central, Hong Kong: the former Central Police Station, the Former Central Magistracy, and the Victoria Prison.

facts.fact: The compound has 16 historic buildings built between 1841 and 1925.
facts.quote: The Former Central Police Station Compound (FCPSC), built between 1841 and 1925, comprises 16 historic buildings grouped under the former Central Police Station, the Former Central Magistracy, and the Victoria Prison.

facts.fact: Victoria Prison was decommissioned in 2006.
facts.quote: Victoria Prison was decommissioned in 2006.

facts.fact: In 2008 the Hong Kong government and the Hong Kong Jockey Club set out to conserve and revitalise the complex; work began in 2011.
facts.quote: In 2008, the government of Hong Kong partnered with the Hong Kong Jockey Club to conserve and revitalise the complex, which turned into one of the most significant and expensive revitalisation projects in the territory, costing HK$1.8 billion; work began in 2011.

facts.fact: It mixes heritage and contemporary architecture, with 16 heritage buildings restored.
facts.quote: Tai Kwun, named after the historical colloquial name of the compound, is a mix of heritage and contemporary architecture, with 16 heritage buildings having been restored.

facts.fact: Two new buildings were added, with designs inspired by the site's historic brickwork.
